Branching & merging::Branching strategie.summary: Branching strategies define which branches remain open, how work moves between development stages, and how short-lived topic branches reach a stable release branch. Git’s documentation contrasts long-running branches with focused topic branches.
Branching & merging::Branching strategie.explanation: Git branching workflows organize development by keeping selected long-running branches for stages such as stable release and integration, while using short-lived topic branches for individual features or related changes. Developers merge topic work into an integration branch and, when stable, promote it to the release branch.

example.title: Use a short-lived topic branch
example.code:
git switch -c feature/login
# edit files and commit changes
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/login
git branch -d feature/login
example.explanation: A short-lived topic branch isolates one feature, then is merged into the stable branch and removed.

useCases.title: Stable releases
useCases.scenario: Keep a release branch stable while work continues elsewhere.

useCases.title: Integration testing
useCases.scenario: Test combined changes before promoting them to production.

useCases.title: Topic development
useCases.scenario: Isolate one feature or bug fix from unrelated work.

keyPoints: Long-running branches can represent distinct development stages, such as integration, testing, and stable release.
A workflow can promote changes progressively by merging from less stable branches into more stable ones.
A release-oriented branch should contain only code considered stable enough for release.
An integration or testing branch can accept ongoing work before it is ready for the stable branch.
Use short-lived topic branches to isolate one feature or a closely related group of changes.
Local branch creation and merging affect the repository only; publishing or sharing requires separate remote operations.
gotchas: Branching and merging locally does not automatically communicate changes to a server or publish a branch; use remote operations when collaboration requires it.

Branching & merging::Fast-forward vs mer.summary: Git fast-forwards when the current branch is an ancestor of the incoming history, moving the branch pointer without creating a commit. Divergent histories require a merge commit; --no-ff can also force one when fast-forwarding is possible.
Branching & merging::Fast-forward vs mer.explanation: When the current branch points to an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git can incorporate the newer history by moving the current branch pointer forward, so no new commit is needed. If both branches contain independent work, Git combines their tips and common ancestor in a three-way merge, then records the result in a merge commit with both branch tips as parents. The --no-ff option forces that commit even when a fast-forward is possible.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: The branch or commit whose history should be merged into the current branch.

parameters.name: --no-ff
parameters.description: Require a merge commit instead of fast-forwarding when possible.

parameters.name: --ff
parameters.description: Allow fast-forwarding when possible; otherwise create a merge commit.

parameters.name: --ff-only
parameters.description: Allow the merge to fast-forward only; fail when a true merge is required.

Branching & merging::Fast-forward vs mer.returns: Updates the current branch by fast-forwarding its pointer or by creating a merge commit; the command can fail when --ff-only is requested but fast-forwarding is impossible.

example.title: Fast-forward and explicit merge commit
example.code:
git switch main
git merge feature
# Force a merge commit when fast-forwarding is possible
git merge --no-ff feature
example.explanation: Run the ordinary merge from the branch that should receive the changes. Add --no-ff when you want Git to create a merge commit even if a fast-forward would work.

useCases.title: Update a branch without adding history
useCases.scenario: The current branch has no independent commits and should simply catch up to a descendant.

useCases.title: Preserve feature merge points
useCases.scenario: A team wants an explicit record for every feature integration, even when histories are linear.

useCases.title: Enforce linear integration
useCases.scenario: A merge should be accepted only when it can move the pointer without combining divergent work.

interview.question: When does Git perform a fast-forward merge?
interview.answer: A fast-forward is possible when the current branch tip is an ancestor of the commit being merged. Git then updates the branch pointer to the newer commit without creating another commit.
interview.followUp: How do you preserve an explicit integration point in that case? Use git merge --no-ff, which creates a merge commit even though a pointer move would suffice.

interview.question: What is a merge commit?
interview.answer: A true merge is needed when the histories have diverged. Git performs a three-way merge and creates a commit whose parents represent the merged branch tips.
interview.followUp: What inputs determine the three-way result? Git uses the two branch-tip snapshots and their common ancestor.

interview.question: How do --ff, --no-ff, and --no-commit relate?
interview.answer: Without extra options, Git prefers a fast-forward when the incoming commit descends from the current commit. --no-ff overrides that preference and creates a merge commit in every case where fast-forwarding would otherwise be possible.
interview.followUp: What does --no-commit change for a fast-forward? Nothing by itself: a fast-forward creates no commit, so combine --no-commit with --no-ff when you need a stoppable merge.

keyPoints: A fast-forward is available when the current branch tip is an ancestor of the commit named for merging.
In a fast-forward, Git updates HEAD and the index to the incoming commit rather than creating a new commit.
Fast-forward integration preserves the existing commit chain and adds no merge node.
After histories diverge, the resulting merge commit has both merged branch tips as parents.
Fast-forwarding is Git's default when the incoming commit is a descendant of the current tip.
Use --no-ff to require a merge commit even when Git could simply move the branch pointer.
gotchas: A fast-forward cannot be paused with --no-commit because Git does not create a commit; use --no-ff together with --no-commit when you need to inspect or stop the merge.
The default fast-forward behavior can hide the fact that a branch was integrated; use --no-ff when preserving an explicit merge record matters.

Branching & merging::git checkout.summary: `git checkout` switches branches, restores selected files, creates branches, and can check out commits with detached HEAD. It updates HEAD, the index, and the working tree according to the selected mode.
Branching & merging::git checkout.explanation: `git checkout` operates in branch-switching and file-restoration modes. With a branch, it updates HEAD, the index, and the working tree; with a commit or tree plus paths, it replaces selected files. Branch creation, detached HEAD operation, merge-conflict handling, and interactive patch selection are available through options.
Branching & merging::git checkout.syntax:
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [<branch>]
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] --detach [<branch>]
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [--detach] <commit>
git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [[-b|-B|--orphan] <new-branch>] [<start-point>]
git checkout [-f|--ours|--theirs|-m|--conflict=<style>] [<tree-ish>] [--] <paths>…​
git checkout [-p|--patch] [<tree-ish>] [--] [<paths>…​]

parameters.name: <branch> / <commit> / <tree-ish>
parameters.description: Branch, commit, or tree object to check out; may also identify a starting point for branch creation.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: Name of the branch to create, reset, or check out.

parameters.name: <start-point>
parameters.description: Optional revision from which a new branch is created.

parameters.name: <paths>
parameters.description: Files or pathspecs to restore from the index or specified tree.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling quiet output, force, merge behavior, detachment, patch selection, and conflict style.

Branching & merging::git checkout.returns: Updates HEAD, the index, and/or working-tree files; on success, the selected branch becomes current or the requested paths are restored. The command exits nonzero when the requested checkout cannot be completed.

example.title: Switch branches and restore a file
example.code:
git switch -c feature/login
printf 'login' > login.txt
git add login.txt
git commit -m 'Add login placeholder'
git checkout main
git checkout feature/login -- login.txt
example.explanation: Creates and commits a feature branch, returns to main, then restores one file from the feature branch.

useCases.title: Switch branches
useCases.scenario: Move from one development line to another while retaining compatible local edits.

useCases.title: Create a branch
useCases.scenario: Start work from an existing commit or branch with a new branch name.

useCases.title: Detached inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect a historical commit without changing a branch reference.

useCases.title: Restore paths
useCases.scenario: Recover or compare selected files from a commit, branch, or index.

interview.question: What are the two main uses of `git checkout`?
interview.answer: It has two primary modes: switching branches and restoring a file version. A branch argument updates HEAD and the working tree; a tree or commit followed by paths restores selected files.
interview.followUp: How can a file be restored from another branch? Use `git checkout <branch> -- <path>`; the `--` separates the tree name from the pathspec.

interview.question: How do you create and switch to a branch with checkout?
interview.answer: `git checkout -b <new-branch> [<start-point>]` creates a branch and checks it out. Without a start point, the branch starts from the current HEAD.
interview.followUp: How does `-B` differ? It creates or resets the named branch to the start point before checking it out, potentially moving an existing branch.

interview.question: What does detached HEAD mean with `git checkout`?
interview.answer: Checking out a commit places HEAD directly at that commit instead of on a branch. This is detached HEAD mode, useful for inspection or temporary experiments; commits should be given a branch name if they must be retained.
interview.followUp: How do you explicitly request detached mode while naming a branch starting point? Use `git checkout --detach <branch>` or its equivalent syntax.

keyPoints: The command can move the current checkout to a branch or replace working-tree files with versions from the index or a tree.
When restoring without a tree argument, checkout takes file contents from the index.
Branch switching makes the selected branch the current branch by moving HEAD to that branch reference.
Compatible uncommitted changes generally remain when switching branches.
The `-b` form creates a new branch from the optional start point and checks it out.
The `--detach` form checks out a starting branch or commit without attaching HEAD to a branch.
Patch mode interactively selects portions of changes to restore rather than restoring every selected path.
gotchas: Switching normally preserves local changes, but checkout can refuse when changes would be overwritten; use `-f` only when discarding those changes is intentional.

Branching & merging::git merge.summary: Merge incorporates one or more commits into the currently checked-out branch. Git fast-forwards when possible; when histories have diverged, it can create a merge commit joining them.
Branching & merging::git merge.explanation: Run the command while checked out on the branch that should receive the changes. Git incorporates the named commit or branch from the point where histories diverged; it may fast-forward when possible, or create a merge commit when both sides contain new commits. If automatic merging cannot finish, resolve the marked files, stage them, and continue or abort.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling commit creation, statistics, verification, strategy, signing, unrelated histories, messages, and other merge behavior.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: One or more commits, usually branch heads, whose changes should be merged into the current branch.

parameters.name: --continue
parameters.description: Resume a merge after conflicts have been resolved and staged.

parameters.name: --abort
parameters.description: Attempt to return to the state before the merge began.

parameters.name: --quit
parameters.description: Stop the merge operation while leaving the index and working tree state intact.

Branching & merging::git merge.returns: Updates the current branch with the merged history, normally creating a commit when needed; on conflict, leaves the merge paused for resolution.

example.title: Merge a feature branch
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

git switch main
git merge feature/login

git log --oneline --graph --decorate -5
example.explanation: Switch to the destination branch, merge the feature branch, then inspect the resulting history.

useCases.title: Combine branch work
useCases.scenario: Integrate completed work from a topic branch into the checked-out development branch.

useCases.title: Integrate remote updates
useCases.scenario: Bring changes from a fetched remote branch into the local branch.

useCases.title: Review a pending merge
useCases.scenario: Pause before committing to inspect or refine the merged tree.

useCases.title: Complete a conflict resolution
useCases.scenario: Resolve divergent edits while preserving both lines of history.

interview.question: Which branch receives the merged changes, and when is a merge commit created?
interview.answer: The current branch is the destination: merge incorporates changes from the named commits into it. Git can fast-forward if the destination has not diverged; otherwise it creates a commit with both histories as parents.
interview.followUp: How do you finish a conflicted merge? Edit the marked files, run git add on each resolved file, then use git merge --continue or git commit.

interview.question: What does --no-commit do, and what limitation does it have?
interview.answer: git merge --no-commit performs the merge but stops before creating the commit, allowing inspection or edits. It cannot stop a fast-forward, because a fast-forward does not create a merge commit.
interview.followUp: How can a merge commit be forced when a fast-forward is possible? Use --no-ff.

interview.question: How are merge conflicts completed or abandoned?
interview.answer: When automatic resolution fails, Git leaves conflict markers in the working tree and stops. Resolve the files, stage them with git add, and seal the result with git merge --continue or git commit.
interview.followUp: What if the merge should be abandoned? Run git merge --abort; Git attempts to reconstruct the pre-merge state.

keyPoints: The command brings changes from one or more named commits into whichever branch is currently checked out.
git pull uses merge to integrate fetched changes, and the command can also be run directly.
Normal operation completes the merge and records the result in a commit when the histories require one.
Arguments identify the commits to integrate; branch names commonly resolve to branch-tip commits.
Conflicting files are marked in the working tree so you can edit them into a consistent result.
After staging conflict resolutions, finish the paused merge with either git commit or git merge --continue.
gotchas: An unresolved conflict pauses the operation; resolve the files and stage the results before continuing, or abort the merge.
Use --no-commit when you need to inspect or adjust the merged result before committing.
The default commit behavior can override --no-commit when explicitly requested with --commit.

Branching & merging::git merge --abort.summary: `git merge --abort` abandons a merge in progress and attempts to restore the pre-merge state. It is primarily used after conflicts stop the merge.
Branching & merging::git merge --abort.explanation: When a merge is in progress, `git merge --abort` stops conflict resolution and attempts to reconstruct the state from before the merge began. If Git created an autostash, the command reapplies it to the worktree; pre-existing uncommitted changes may not always be recoverable.
Branching & merging::git merge --abort.returns: Aborts the current merge process and attempts to reconstruct the pre-merge state; the page does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Abort a conflicted merge
example.code:
git merge feature/login
# If conflicts stop the merge:
git merge --abort
example.explanation: Run the command after a conflicted merge to abandon the merge and restore the pre-merge state as far as Git can reconstruct it.

useCases.title: Discard a conflicted merge
useCases.scenario: A merge produces conflicts that should not be resolved.

useCases.title: Restore an autostashed worktree
useCases.scenario: An in-progress merge was started with local work already stashed automatically.

useCases.title: Return to the earlier state
useCases.scenario: A merge must be abandoned while preserving the intended pre-merge state.

interview.question: What does `git merge --abort` do?
interview.answer: It aborts the current merge conflict-resolution process and attempts to reconstruct the pre-merge state. It is used while a merge is in progress.
interview.followUp: What happens to an autostash? If one exists, `git merge --abort` applies it back to the worktree.

interview.question: What is the main data-loss risk?
interview.answer: The command can be unable to reconstruct changes that were uncommitted when the merge began. Git therefore recommends committing or stashing changes before running a merge.
interview.followUp: How can you lower that risk? Create a commit or stash the worktree before initiating the merge.

interview.question: How does it compare with `git reset --merge`?
interview.answer: When `MERGE_HEAD` is present, it is equivalent to `git reset --merge` unless `MERGE_AUTOSTASH` is also present. With an autostash, abort reapplies the stash, while reset saves it in the stash list.
interview.followUp: What state indicates an active merge? `MERGE_HEAD` being present indicates the merge state relevant to this equivalence.

keyPoints: Use it to abandon the current conflict-resolution process and restore the earlier merge state.
An existing autostash is reapplied to the worktree during the abort.
A merge can remain in progress when Git cannot resolve a conflict automatically.
After a merge stops, choose abort to abandon it or continue after resolving conflicts.
Without an autostash, abort has the same effect as reset --merge while MERGE_HEAD exists.
gotchas: Abort may not fully restore uncommitted worktree changes that existed when the merge started.
Commit or stash local changes before starting a merge to reduce the risk of losing or misreconstructing them.
With an autostash, abort reapplies the stash, unlike `reset --merge`, which leaves the changes in the stash list.

Branching & merging::git merge --squash.summary: `git merge --squash` applies another branch’s combined changes to the current branch without committing them. You can then inspect or modify the staged result and create one ordinary commit.
Branching & merging::git merge --squash.explanation: Run the command while on the branch that should receive the changes. Git updates the working tree and index as though the named commit or branch were merged, but leaves the result uncommitted; create the final single commit separately.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: Optional commit, branch, or other revision whose changes should be incorporated into the current branch.

Branching & merging::git merge --squash.returns: Updates the working tree and index with the merge result, without creating a commit or recording merge metadata.

example.title: Squash a feature branch into one commit
example.code:
git switch main
git merge --squash feature/login
git commit -m "Add login feature"
example.explanation: Apply the feature branch’s combined changes to the current branch, inspect or adjust them if needed, then create one ordinary commit.

useCases.title: Condense feature history
useCases.scenario: A feature branch contains several implementation commits, but the target branch should receive one clean commit.

useCases.title: Review before committing
useCases.scenario: The merge result needs review or minor edits before it becomes part of the target branch.

useCases.title: Avoid merge metadata
useCases.scenario: A project wants the content of a branch without adding a merge commit and its parent metadata.

interview.question: What does git merge --squash do?
interview.answer: It applies the other branch’s net changes to the current branch without creating a commit. The resulting files are staged in the index, so a later commit can record them as one ordinary commit.
interview.followUp: What merge metadata is omitted? The operation does not move HEAD or record MERGE_HEAD, so the later commit is not a merge commit.

interview.question: How does squash merging affect history?
interview.answer: The current branch receives the working-tree and index state that a merge would produce, but the individual source commits are not recorded in the current branch’s history. The final commit is made explicitly afterward.
interview.followUp: Can the result be changed before committing? Yes: inspect or edit the working tree and index before creating the single commit.

interview.question: How would you use the option in practice?
interview.answer: The command accepts the same commit or branch target form shown by git merge, such as git merge --squash feature. It must be run from the branch intended to receive the changes.
interview.followUp: What happens if --commit is also supplied? Git rejects the command because --squash requires the result to remain uncommitted.

keyPoints: Git prepares both the working tree and index with the merge result, allowing the combined changes to be reviewed before committing.
The operation leaves history unchanged until you explicitly commit; it neither advances HEAD nor records merge-parent metadata.
After the squash operation, one ordinary commit can represent the combined effect on the current branch.
The resulting content has the effect of merging the selected branch, while its separate commits are not individually added.
The inverse option, --no-squash, performs the normal merge-and-commit behavior instead of leaving a squash result uncommitted.
gotchas: Do not combine --squash with --commit; Git rejects that combination.

Branching & merging::git switch.summary: Switch to an existing branch, or create a branch and switch to it. Unlike git checkout, git switch focuses on changing the current branch while also supporting detached and orphan histories.
Branching & merging::git switch.explanation: Use git switch to move the worktree and index to an existing branch, or combine branch creation with the move. It can also detach HEAD, create an orphan branch, or choose a different starting point; Git stops when switching would overwrite local changes unless an option explicitly handles them.
Branching & merging::git switch.syntax:
git switch [<options>] [--no-guess] <branch>
git switch [<options>] --detach [<start-point>]
git switch [<options>] (-c|-C) <new-branch> [<start-point>]
git switch [<options>] --orphan <new-branch>

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling switching, branch creation, guessing, detachment, orphan creation, and handling local changes.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: Existing branch to select.

parameters.name: <start-point>
parameters.description: Commit or other history location used for detached HEAD or as the new branch base.

parameters.name: <new-branch>
parameters.description: Name of the branch to create, or the orphan branch to create.

Branching & merging::git switch.returns: On success, the worktree and index are updated and the selected or newly created branch becomes current; the command reports an error and does not switch when the operation would lose local changes unless an applicable option permits it.

example.title: Create and switch to a branch
example.code:
git switch -c feature/login
printf 'ready\n'
example.explanation: Creates feature/login from the current commit and switches the worktree to it; the second command is a harmless runnable check.

useCases.title: Change branches
useCases.scenario: Move between existing lines of development without using checkout's file-oriented behavior.

useCases.title: Create and select a branch
useCases.scenario: Start feature work from the current commit or a specified revision.

useCases.title: Detached inspection
useCases.scenario: Examine or experiment from a commit without attaching HEAD to a branch.

useCases.title: Orphan branch
useCases.scenario: Start a branch whose initial history is independent of the current history.

interview.question: What does git switch do?
interview.answer: git switch changes the current branch and updates both the working tree and index to match it. New commits then advance the selected branch.
interview.followUp: How can you create and select a branch in one command? Use git switch -c <new-branch> [<start-point>], or -C when resetting an existing branch name is intended.

interview.question: How do you create a branch and move to it?
interview.answer: Use git switch -c <new-branch> [<start-point>]. The optional start point makes the new branch begin at a history location other than the current HEAD.
interview.followUp: How do you create a branch without switching to it? Use git branch; unlike switch -c, that command leaves the worktree on the current branch.

interview.question: How do you inspect a commit without switching to a branch?
interview.answer: git switch --detach [<start-point>] checks out a commit without putting HEAD on a branch. Later commits made there are not added to a named branch unless one is created or another reference is updated.
interview.followUp: What is the orphan form used for? git switch --orphan <new-branch> creates an initially unrelated branch, useful when its history should not inherit the current branch.

keyPoints: With git switch <branch>, Git selects an existing branch and makes it the current branch.
The command synchronizes the files in the worktree and the staging area with the selected branch.
After switching, ordinary commits advance the selected branch rather than the branch previously active.
Use -c to create and switch to a branch, or -C when the named branch may already exist and should be reset.
When configured guessing applies, a same-named remote branch can provide the local branch's starting point.
The --detach form moves to a commit or other start point while leaving HEAD unattached to a branch.
gotchas: Switching can fail when the target would overwrite local changes; use --discard-changes or --merge only when their documented behavior is appropriate.
A clean worktree is not required, but preserving local changes still constrains which switches are safe.

Branching & merging::git tag.summary: git tag assigns a stable name to a Git object, most often a commit. It can create lightweight, annotated, or signed tags, and can also list, delete, or verify them.
Branching & merging::git tag.explanation: A tag is a reference that gives a stable name to an object, commonly a commit. Use the creation form to make a lightweight tag or add -a, -s, or -u to create an annotated or signed tag; supply a commit or object to tag something other than HEAD. The same command can list, delete, or verify tags with -l, -d, or -v.
Branching & merging::git tag.syntax:
git tag [-a | -s | -u <key-id>] [-f] [-m <msg> | -F <file>] [-e] [<tagname> [<commit> | <object>]]
git tag -d <tagname>…
git tag [-n[<num>]] -l [<pattern>…]
git tag -v <tagname>…

parameters.name: <tagname>
parameters.description: Name assigned to the tag.

parameters.name: <commit> | <object>
parameters.description: Commit or other Git object to reference; defaults to HEAD when omitted.

parameters.name: <msg> | <file>
parameters.description: Message for an annotated tag; -F reads the message from a file.

parameters.name: <pattern>
parameters.description: Pattern used to filter listed tag names.

Branching & merging::git tag.returns: Creates, lists, deletes, or verifies tag references or tag objects; the command has no documented value return.

example.title: Create and inspect a release tag
example.code:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"
git show v1.0.0
git tag --list
example.explanation: Creates an annotated tag for the current commit, displays its metadata and target, then lists available tags.

useCases.title: Release versioning
useCases.scenario: Mark a published software release with an immutable-looking human-readable name and release metadata.

useCases.title: Local investigation markers
useCases.scenario: Create a temporary local name for a commit while investigating history.

useCases.title: History and reachability queries
useCases.scenario: Find tags that contain, exclude, or directly reference selected commits.

interview.question: What is the difference between lightweight and annotated tags?
interview.answer: git tag names an object through a reference under refs/tags/. Without annotation options it creates a lightweight tag; -a creates an annotated tag object that stores metadata and a message.
interview.followUp: How would you identify tags that point at a particular commit? Use git tag --points-at <object>.

interview.question: Which commit does git tag mark when no commit is supplied?
interview.answer: The creation form accepts an optional <commit> or <object>; if omitted, the tag targets the current HEAD. A tag can therefore mark an earlier commit by naming that commit explicitly.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the object and metadata behind a tag? Run git show <tagname>.

interview.question: What operations besides creating a tag does git tag provide?
interview.answer: The command supports multiple operations: -l lists tags, -d deletes existing tags, and -v verifies signed tags. Listing can also filter by containment, target object, merge status, pattern, sorting, or format.
interview.followUp: How can you list tags reachable from a commit but exclude tags whose commits are reachable from another? Combine --contains and --no-contains filters.

keyPoints: The default operation creates a tag reference; the command switches to deletion, listing, or verification when those modes are selected.
Use -a or --annotate when the tag should carry annotation data rather than merely naming an object.
Use -s or --sign to create a signed tag with the configured default key.
gotchas: Choose annotated tags for releases; lightweight tags are better suited to temporary or local labels.

Branching & merging::Resolving merge con.summary: Resolve files Git could not merge automatically by editing them into the intended combined result, staging them, and completing the merge. If you do not want to proceed, abort the merge instead.
Branching & merging::Resolving merge con.explanation: When Git cannot combine changes automatically, it leaves conflicts in the working tree. Edit each affected file into the desired combined form, stage the resolved paths, and finish with a commit or git merge --continue; use git merge --abort instead if you decide to abandon the merge.

example.title: Resolve and complete a merge
example.code:
git switch main
git merge feature
# Edit conflicted files, removing conflict markers
git add path/to/resolved-file
git merge --continue
example.explanation: Resolve each conflicted file, stage the chosen content, then complete the merge.

useCases.title: Manual conflict resolution
useCases.scenario: A merge stops because changes to the same area cannot be combined automatically.

useCases.title: Inspecting competing changes
useCases.scenario: You need to compare the current state with both merge parents.

useCases.title: Using a mergetool
useCases.scenario: A graphical workflow is preferable for reviewing and combining file versions.

useCases.title: Aborting the merge
useCases.scenario: The conflict is unexpected and the merge should be postponed.

interview.question: What is the normal workflow for resolving a merge conflict?
interview.answer: Git stops the merge and marks conflicting paths in the working tree. Edit those files to the intended combined result, stage them with git add, and finish with git commit or git merge --continue.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the competing changes? Use git diff for a three-way diff between the HEAD and MERGE_HEAD versions.

interview.question: How do you back out of a merge with conflicts?
interview.answer: git merge --abort cancels the in-progress merge and attempts to restore the pre-merge state. It is the documented choice when you decide not to merge.
interview.followUp: What should you do if you still want the merge later? Recreate or retry the merge after preparing the working tree as needed.

interview.question: What alternatives does Git document for examining or resolving conflicts?
interview.answer: git mergetool launches a graphical merge tool that helps work through the conflict. After choosing the desired content, the resolved files still need to be staged and the merge completed.
interview.followUp: How can you review resolution progress without a graphical tool? git diff AUTO_MERGE shows changes made so far to resolve textual conflicts.

keyPoints: Choose the correct combined content for every conflicted file rather than automatically favoring one side.
Modify each conflicted file, remove the conflict markers, and stage the finished result with git add.
Once all conflicts are staged, complete the merge with a commit or the continuation command.
Use git diff to compare the current merge result with both sides of the conflict.
Use the AUTO_MERGE diff to review your resolution work before completing the merge.
A graphical mergetool can guide resolution when manually comparing the versions is inconvenient.
gotchas: Do not assume a conflicted file is resolved merely because it has been edited; inspect it and stage the final content.
If the merge should be abandoned, abort it rather than attempting to complete it with unresolved paths.

Getting started::.gitignore.summary: Use .gitignore patterns to keep selected untracked files and directories out of Git. Rules can be repository-wide, nested, or user-specific, but they do not affect paths Git already tracks.
Getting started::.gitignore.explanation: A .gitignore file contains one pattern per line for paths that should remain untracked. Git can read ignore rules from a repository .gitignore, a per-repository exclude file, and a user-wide exclude file; rules are pattern-based, and more specific locations or later matching rules can override earlier ones. Ignore rules do not affect files already tracked.

example.title: Ignore generated and local files
example.code:
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
# Build output
build/
dist/

# Local secrets
.env

# Editor files
*.swp

# Keep this generated file despite the wildcard
!important.log
EOF

git status --short
example.explanation: Create the file in the repository root, then inspect the short status to confirm matching untracked paths are omitted.

useCases.title: Exclude generated files
useCases.scenario: Prevent compiler output, package bundles, caches, and temporary editor files from appearing as untracked changes.

useCases.title: Exclude local configuration
useCases.scenario: Keep machine-local configuration and development credentials out of commits by matching their filenames or locations.

useCases.title: Scope rules by directory
useCases.scenario: Add repository-wide defaults in a root file and refine them for subdirectories with nested ignore files.

useCases.title: Create exceptions
useCases.scenario: Use a negated pattern to make a specific exception to a broader ignore rule when the parent directory remains traversable.

interview.question: What does .gitignore do, and what does it not do?
interview.answer: A .gitignore file lists patterns for files Git should intentionally leave untracked. It does not change the status of files that are already tracked.
interview.followUp: How would you stop tracking an already committed secret while keeping it locally? Remove it from the index, add a matching ignore pattern, and separately consider rewriting history if the secret was exposed.

interview.question: Where can Git obtain ignore patterns?
interview.answer: Git can read patterns from command-line sources, a .gitignore in the relevant directory hierarchy, the repository's info/exclude file, and a user-wide exclude file. Within one precedence level, the last matching pattern wins.
interview.followUp: Which repository-local ignore mechanism avoids sharing a pattern with collaborators? Use $GIT_DIR/info/exclude, because it is repository-local but is not a committed .gitignore file.

interview.question: How do slashes change a pattern's scope?
interview.answer: A pattern without a slash can match at any directory level. A leading slash anchors a pattern to the directory containing the .gitignore, while a trailing slash makes the pattern match directories.
interview.followUp: How can a rule ignore build directories recursively but not a file named build? Use build/; the trailing slash specifies a directory.

keyPoints: Use the file to keep selected untracked paths out of normal Git operations.
Write one ignore pattern per line; blank lines and comments are not matching rules.
A .gitignore can apply to paths in its directory and descendants, with nested files able to refine the rules.
For repository .gitignore files, rules closer to the path take precedence over rules in parent directories.
gotchas: Adding a tracked file to .gitignore does not stop tracking it; remove it from the index separately if that is intended.
When multiple patterns at the same precedence match, the final matching pattern determines whether the path is ignored.
A negation pattern cannot restore a file when one of its parent directories is already excluded.

Getting started::git add.summary: Stage new or changed content in Git’s index so you can control exactly what the next commit contains. Use paths for whole files or patch mode for selected changes.
Getting started::git add.explanation: `git add` copies the current contents of specified working-tree files into Git’s index, also called the staging area. The index records what the next commit will contain, so you can stage files or selected hunks and repeat the command as your work evolves.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling verbosity, previewing, forcing, interaction, patch selection, update behavior, normalization, permissions, and pathspec input.

parameters.name: pathspec
parameters.description: Files or paths whose current contents should be added to the index.

Getting started::git add.returns: Updates the index; the documentation does not specify a separate return value.

example.title: Stage selected changes
example.code:
git add -p src/app.js

git status

git commit -m "Update app behavior"
example.explanation: Interactively choose the hunks from a modified file to stage, inspect the staged set, then commit exactly that selection.

useCases.title: Stage selected paths
useCases.scenario: Prepare a focused commit from several changed files.

useCases.title: Stage individual hunks
useCases.scenario: Separate unrelated edits in one file into different commits.

useCases.title: Dry-run staging
useCases.scenario: Preview the effect of staging before changing the index.

useCases.title: Force-add an ignored path
useCases.scenario: Include a deliberately ignored file in a commit.

interview.question: What does `git add` do?
interview.answer: `git add` updates the index from the current contents of files in the working tree. The index is the staging area used to prepare the next commit, so staging determines what that commit will contain.
interview.followUp: How can one file contribute only part of its changes? Use `git add --patch` to select individual hunks interactively.

interview.question: Does staging automatically track later edits?
interview.answer: A file can be staged, edited again, and staged again before committing. Each invocation records the file’s contents at that moment, allowing the index to be revised incrementally.
interview.followUp: How would you verify which changes are staged? Run `git status`, which summarizes files with changes staged for the next commit.

interview.question: How do you stage only selected work?
interview.answer: Use a pathspec to limit staging to particular files or paths, such as `git add src/app.js`. For selective portions of a file, use the patch mode option.
interview.followUp: What if a file is ignored but must be included? Add it with `git add --force <path>` after confirming that inclusion is intentional.

keyPoints: The command stages new or modified file contents in Git’s index.
The index is the staging area that defines the content prepared for the next commit.
You may run `git add` repeatedly before committing as you refine the staged set.
Patch mode lets you stage only selected portions of a changed file.
Use `git status` to review which files currently have staged changes.
gotchas: Staging is a snapshot: later edits to a staged file are not included automatically; run `git add` again.
Ignored files are skipped normally; use `--force` only when intentionally staging one.

Getting started::git clone.summary: Copies a repository into a new directory, including its history and remote-tracking branches. It also creates and checks out an initial branch based on the source repository’s active branch.
Getting started::git clone.explanation: Git creates a new directory from the repository, obtains its history, records the remote, creates remote-tracking branches for the repository’s branches, and checks out an initial branch based on the source repository’s currently active branch.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: The repository to clone, such as a URL or local repository path.

parameters.name: <directory>
parameters.description: Optional destination directory; if supplied, Git creates the clone there.

parameters.name: -b <name>
parameters.description: Optional branch to check out after cloning.

Getting started::git clone.returns: A newly created local clone containing the repository and its history, with remote-tracking branches and an initial checked-out branch.

example.title: Clone a repository
example.code:
git clone https://github.com/example/project.git project
cd project
git branch --remotes
example.explanation: Clones the repository into the named directory, enters it, and lists the remote-tracking branches created by the clone.

useCases.title: Get a local working copy
useCases.scenario: Starting work on an existing project

useCases.title: Prepare a development checkout
useCases.scenario: Reviewing or contributing to a remote project

useCases.title: Name the clone directory
useCases.scenario: Creating a local copy with a chosen destination

useCases.title: Explore remote-tracking branches
useCases.scenario: Inspecting branches from the source repository

interview.question: What does git clone create?
interview.answer: It creates a new directory containing the repository, its history, remote-tracking branches, and an initially checked-out branch forked from the source repository’s active branch.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect the remote-tracking branches? Run git branch --remotes.

interview.question: What is the basic syntax of git clone?
interview.answer: The command accepts a repository location and an optional destination directory. If the directory is omitted, Git derives the new directory name from the repository location.
interview.followUp: How can you choose a different destination? Provide it as the optional directory argument.

interview.question: How do you choose the branch checked out after cloning?
interview.answer: The -b option selects a branch for the initial checkout instead of relying on the source repository’s currently active branch.
interview.followUp: What does cloning still create for other source branches? It creates remote-tracking branches for them.

keyPoints: The command copies a repository into a newly created working directory.
The destination is created as part of the clone operation rather than requiring an existing project directory.
The clone records remote-tracking counterparts for the source repository’s branches.
Use git branch --remotes to display the remote-tracking branches produced by cloning.
Cloning both creates an initial local branch and switches the working tree to it.
By default, the initial local branch derives from the source repository’s active branch.
gotchas: The checked-out initial branch follows the source repository’s currently active branch; it is not necessarily a branch name you choose unless you use an option such as -b.
Remote-tracking branches are created for the source branches, but they are distinct from local branches.

Getting started::git commit.summary: Creates a new commit from the staged contents in the index and records a message describing the changes. The commit normally follows HEAD and advances the current branch.
Getting started::git commit.explanation: Git builds a new commit from the current contents of the index and the supplied log message. That commit normally becomes a direct child of HEAD, and the current branch moves to it; with detached HEAD, no branch reference is advanced.

parameters.name: <file>…
parameters.description: Optional pathspecs selecting files whose current contents should be committed instead of using the index for those paths.

parameters.name: <msg>
parameters.description: Text supplied as the commit log message.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: A commit object used by options such as --amend or --fixup.

Getting started::git commit.returns: Creates a new commit and normally updates the current branch to point to it.

example.title: Commit staged changes
example.code:
git add src/app.js
git commit -m "Add application startup"
example.explanation: Stages the selected file, then creates a commit from the index with an explicit message.

useCases.title: Create a normal commit
useCases.scenario: You have reviewed a coherent set of staged edits and want to preserve them as one history entry.

useCases.title: Commit selected staged changes
useCases.scenario: You need to build a commit from only part of the work currently present in the working tree.

useCases.title: Record a file removal
useCases.scenario: A tracked file should be removed and that removal included in the next history entry.

interview.question: What does git commit record?
interview.answer: The command creates a commit from the index, not from every change in the working tree. The log message describes the resulting commit, which is normally made directly after HEAD.
interview.followUp: What happens to unstaged edits? They remain in the working tree and are not part of the commit unless the command's selected-file behavior or another option includes them.

interview.question: How do you choose which changes are committed?
interview.answer: Use git add to incrementally place changes in the index, then run git commit with a message such as -m. The index is the source of the new commit's contents.
interview.followUp: Why can a modified file be absent from the commit? Because it was changed in the working tree but not added to the index.

interview.question: What reference moves after a commit?
interview.answer: The new commit is normally a direct child of HEAD, and the current branch is updated to point at it. If the working tree has detached HEAD, no branch is associated with it, so no branch name advances.
interview.followUp: How can a commit affect only selected paths? Supplying file arguments makes Git record those files' current contents and ignore staged index changes for those paths.

keyPoints: The commit snapshots what is currently staged in the index.
A commit includes a log message that records the purpose or description of its changes.
A normal commit extends the current history by placing the new commit immediately after HEAD.
HEAD ordinarily identifies the latest commit on the checked-out branch.
Stage changes incrementally with git add before creating the commit.
Use git rm when removing a tracked file should affect both the working tree and the staged snapshot.
gotchas: Ordinary modifications are not included merely because they exist in the working tree; stage them before committing.
When file paths are supplied to the command, Git uses those files' current contents instead of the staged index for them.
A normal commit advances the current branch, but a detached HEAD has no branch reference to move.

Getting started::git config.summary: Read and set Git configuration variables at repository, user, or system scope. These settings control how Git commands behave.
Getting started::git config.explanation: `git config` reads or changes named Git variables. Without a scope option, writes normally target the current repository; `--global` targets user-wide settings, while `--system` targets system-wide defaults. Git combines configuration files, with repository values serving as overrides for user-level fallback values.

parameters.name: <name>
parameters.description: Configuration variable name, such as `user.name` or `core.editor`.

parameters.name: <value>
parameters.description: Value assigned to the named configuration variable; omit it when reading.

parameters.name: <file-option>
parameters.description: Selects the configuration file or scope, such as `--global`, `--system`, `--local`, `--worktree`, or `--file`.

parameters.name: <value-pattern>
parameters.description: Optional value pattern used by operations that select or modify matching entries.

Getting started::git config.returns: When reading, prints the requested configuration value; when writing, updates the selected configuration file.

example.title: Set and read user identity
example.code:
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
git config user.name
example.explanation: Sets the author identity for the current user, then reads the configured name from the applicable configuration.

useCases.title: Set user identity
useCases.scenario: Configure author identity once for all repositories on a machine.

useCases.title: Set repository-specific behavior
useCases.scenario: Override a default only in one project.

useCases.title: Diagnose configuration
useCases.scenario: Inspect where a setting comes from when multiple scopes are involved.

useCases.title: Set system-wide defaults
useCases.scenario: Apply organization-wide defaults for all users.

keyPoints: Use `git config` to read existing settings or assign new values that control Git's behavior.
Configuration variables change how Git commands operate, such as identity, defaults, and behavior options.
Repository-specific configuration is stored in `.git/config`, with optional worktree-specific settings available.
User-level settings provide defaults that repositories can inherit unless they define their own values.
System-level configuration supplies defaults across the installation and its users.
Add `--global` when a setting should apply to the current user instead of only the current repository.
gotchas: System-wide settings affect all users and repositories, so use them only when that broad scope is intentional.
A repository setting can override a user-level value; inspect the repository scope when a global setting appears ineffective.

Getting started::git diff.summary: git diff displays changes between Git states, including the working tree, index, commits, branches, trees, blobs, and filesystem paths. Its arguments determine which two states are compared.
Getting started::git diff.explanation: Git compares selected repository states and prints their differences. With no commit argument, it compares the working tree with the index; --cached compares the index with HEAD, while two commits compare those trees. The -- separator makes following arguments paths rather than revisions.
Getting started::git diff.syntax:
git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] --cached [<commit>] [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] <commit> <commit> [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>…]
git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path>

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Optional diff-format and comparison options, such as --cached, --no-index, --merge-base, -U<n>, and --raw.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: A revision, such as HEAD, a commit ID, or a branch name, used as a comparison tree.

parameters.name: <commit> <commit>
parameters.description: Two revisions or a revision range for comparing repository trees.

parameters.name: <path>…
parameters.description: Paths to limit the comparison; after -- they are interpreted as paths.

Getting started::git diff.returns: A textual diff describing changes between the selected trees, working files, index, blobs, or filesystem paths.

example.title: Compare working-tree and staged changes
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
printf 'one\n' > file.txt
git add file.txt
git commit -m 'initial'
printf 'one\ntwo\n' > file.txt
git diff
git add file.txt
git diff --cached
 git diff HEAD
example.explanation: This runnable shell sequence shows unstaged changes, staged changes, and the combined difference from the latest commit.

useCases.title: Inspect unstaged work
useCases.scenario: Review edits before staging them.

useCases.title: Review staged work
useCases.scenario: Check exactly what the next commit would contain.

useCases.title: Compare repository histories
useCases.scenario: Examine changes introduced by a commit, branch, or range.

useCases.title: Compare filesystem paths
useCases.scenario: Inspect differences between generated or unrelated files.

interview.question: What do git diff and git diff --cached compare?
interview.answer: With no commit arguments, git diff compares the working tree with the index, so it displays unstaged changes. git diff --cached instead compares the index with HEAD and displays what is staged for the next commit.
interview.followUp: How do you compare a branch with its common ancestor? Use git diff A...B; it is equivalent to comparing the merge base of A and B with B.

interview.question: How do you compare two commits or restrict the result to files?
interview.answer: git diff A B compares the trees represented by the two commits. A path restriction after -- limits the output to selected paths, and the separator disambiguates paths from revision arguments.
interview.followUp: How can two files outside Git be compared? Use git diff --no-index path1 path2.

interview.question: How can you compare the working tree with another commit or branch?
interview.answer: git diff <commit> compares the working tree with the named commit. Using HEAD compares the working tree with the latest commit, while a branch name compares it with that branch tip.
interview.followUp: What does git diff A...B show? It shows changes from their common ancestor through B, rather than a direct A-to-B comparison.

keyPoints: The command can compare working-tree files, the staging area, commits or other tree objects.
Use --no-index to compare two filesystem paths, including paths that are not repository versions.
The unstaged differences reported by plain git diff can be moved into the index with git add.
The -U<n> option changes how many surrounding unchanged lines appear in each diff hunk.
A three-dot comparison uses the merge base of the revisions as its left side and the second revision as its right side.
gotchas: Plain git diff does not show changes already staged; use git diff --cached for the index-to-HEAD comparison.
The three-dot form compares from the merge base to the second commit, not the complete contents of both named commits.

Getting started::git init.summary: Turn a directory into an empty Git repository by creating its Git metadata, normally in .git. It also creates an initial branch with no commits, and can initialize a chosen directory or a bare repository.
Getting started::git init.explanation: Run git init in a project directory, or provide a directory argument, to create the repository metadata. Git creates the internal objects, branch-reference, tag-reference, and template areas, plus an initial branch with no commits; an existing repository can be initialized again without overwriting what is already there.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Suppresses all output except errors and warnings.

parameters.name: --bare
parameters.description: Creates a bare repository.

parameters.name: --template=<template-directory>
parameters.description: Directory from which templates are used.

parameters.name: --separate-git-dir=<git-dir>
parameters.description: Stores the actual repository separately from the working tree metadata location.

parameters.name: --object-format=<format>
parameters.description: Selects the repository object hash format.

parameters.name: --ref-format=<format>
parameters.description: Selects the reference storage format.

parameters.name: -b <branch-name>, --initial-branch=<branch-name>
parameters.description: Sets the initial branch name.

parameters.name: --shared[=<permissions>]
parameters.description: Controls shared-repository permissions.

parameters.name: <directory>
parameters.description: Directory to initialize; defaults to the current directory.

Getting started::git init.returns: Creates or reinitializes a Git repository and prints initialization status unless --quiet is used.

example.title: Initialize a new repository
example.code:
mkdir demo && cd demo
git init -b main
printf 'hello\n' > README.md
git status
example.explanation: Creates a directory, initializes it with an explicitly named initial branch, adds a file, and checks the repository state.

useCases.title: Adopt an unversioned project
useCases.scenario: Starting version control for an existing local project folder.

useCases.title: Set the initial branch
useCases.scenario: Selecting a repository's first branch name during setup.

useCases.title: Create a bare repository
useCases.scenario: Creating a repository intended for shared Git transport without a checked-out working tree.

useCases.title: Separate the Git directory
useCases.scenario: Keeping repository metadata outside the project directory.

interview.question: What does git init create?
interview.answer: git init creates an empty repository by creating repository metadata, including areas for objects, heads, tags, and templates. It also creates an initial branch that has no commits.
interview.followUp: What happens when it is run inside an existing repository? It is safe and does not overwrite data that is already present.

interview.question: What does the optional directory argument control?
interview.answer: The directory argument selects where Git initializes the repository; if omitted, Git uses the current directory. The command can therefore initialize either the working directory or a specified directory.
interview.followUp: How can the metadata be stored elsewhere? Use --separate-git-dir to place the actual repository in another location while leaving a file at the normal metadata path.

interview.question: How do you choose the initial branch name?
interview.answer: The -b or --initial-branch option sets the name of the first branch created in the otherwise empty repository. Without that option, the branch name follows Git's configured default behavior.
interview.followUp: How would you create a repository intended only for serving Git data? Add --bare, which creates a bare repository rather than a normal working-tree repository.

keyPoints: A normal initialization creates a .git directory containing Git's object, branch-reference, tag-reference, and template areas.
Initialization creates the first branch before any commit exists.
Use -b or --initial-branch to choose the name of the initial branch.
The --bare option creates a repository without the usual working tree.
--separate-git-dir stores the actual repository elsewhere and leaves a pointer file at the expected location.
gotchas: Re-running the command in an existing repository is safe and does not overwrite existing repository data.
GIT_DIR can redirect repository metadata away from the usual .git location.

Getting started::git log.summary: Read commit history with filtering and formatting controls. Select revisions, exclude ancestors, restrict results to paths, and choose how commits and their changes are displayed.
Getting started::git log.explanation: git log walks commits reachable from the selected starting points, optionally restricting them with a revision range and path. Options control ordering, commit selection, displayed metadata, and the diff or patch information shown for each commit.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling commit selection, ordering, formatting, and displayed changes.

parameters.name: <revision-range>
parameters.description: A revision expression selecting the commits to inspect.

parameters.name: <path>…
parameters.description: One or more paths; only commits affecting these paths are shown.

Getting started::git log.returns: Commit history written to standard output.

example.title: Inspect source history
example.code: git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all -- src/
example.explanation: Displays a compact, decorated graph of commits reachable from all references that changed files under src/.

useCases.title: Browse commits
useCases.scenario: Review recent project history in the default newest-first order.

useCases.title: Compare revision ranges
useCases.scenario: Find commits present locally but absent from a remote-tracking reference.

useCases.title: Trace paths
useCases.scenario: Audit why a file or directory changed over time.

useCases.title: Visualize or simplify history
useCases.scenario: Understand branch structure while omitting integration commits when appropriate.

interview.question: What does `git log` do, and what is its default ordering?
interview.answer: It shows commit logs by traversing parent links from the specified commits. By default, output is in reverse chronological order, and the command can also control displayed changes using diff-related options.
interview.followUp: How would you show only work on the current branch that is absent from origin? Use `git log origin..HEAD`; this selects commits reachable from `HEAD` but not from `origin`.

interview.question: How does a revision range affect the result?
interview.answer: A revision range selects which reachable commits are included. For example, `origin..HEAD` means commits reachable from `HEAD` but not from `origin`.
interview.followUp: How can equivalent exclusions be written explicitly? Use `git log HEAD ^origin`, or use `--not` with the excluded revision.

interview.question: How do you restrict history to particular paths?
interview.answer: Place `--` before paths to distinguish path arguments from revisions: `git log [options] [revision-range] [--] [path]…`. This lets the command show commits that changed selected files or directories.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect changes in two directories? Put both paths after `--`, for example `git log -- include/scsi drivers/scsi`.

keyPoints: The command follows parent links from the supplied commit or commits to determine the history it can list.
Prefixing a revision with `^` excludes commits reachable from that revision.
A revision range narrows the output to commits selected by the range expression.
Many selection and presentation controls come from options also applicable to `git rev-list`.
Diff-family options control how each commit's introduced changes are displayed.
`--no-merges` displays the history while omitting merge commits.
gotchas: Without a revision range, the command examines the complete history leading to the current commit, not every reference in the repository.
The default order is newest commits first; use an ordering option when topology or another order matters.
`--no-merges` removes merge commits from the displayed history, so it can hide important integration points.

Getting started::git status.summary: Shows the working tree status: staged changes, unstaged edits, and untracked files that Git does not ignore. Options provide concise, branch-aware, script-friendly, verbose, or path-limited output.
Getting started::git status.explanation: Run this command inside a Git repository to compare the current commit, staging area, and working tree. It reports staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked files that are not excluded by gitignore; options can select concise, script-stable, branch-aware, verbose, or path-limited output.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Optional command-line switches such as --short, --branch, --porcelain, --verbose, and untracked-file controls.

parameters.name: <pathspec>…
parameters.description: Optional files or directories whose status should be examined.

Getting started::git status.returns: Displays paths differing between HEAD and the index, paths differing between the working tree and index, and untracked paths that are not ignored.

example.title: Inspect staged and unstaged changes
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
echo 'hello' > app.txt
git add app.txt
echo 'world' >> app.txt
git status --short --branch
example.explanation: Creates a repository, stages an initial file, edits it afterward, then displays branch information and separate index/work-tree status codes.

useCases.title: Review what will be committed
useCases.scenario: Before creating a commit

useCases.title: Separate staged from unstaged work
useCases.scenario: After editing tracked files

useCases.title: Parse stable status output
useCases.scenario: In a shell script or CI check

useCases.title: Show branch, tracking, and stash information
useCases.scenario: When checking repository context

interview.question: What does git status report?
interview.answer: It compares three states: HEAD versus the index, the index versus the working tree, and untracked working-tree paths that are not ignored. Thus it distinguishes staged changes from edits that still need staging.
interview.followUp: How would you make output suitable for a script? Use --porcelain, optionally with a specified format version, because the documentation describes it as stable across Git versions and user configuration.

interview.question: What is the command syntax, and how can output be narrowed?
interview.answer: The synopsis is `git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>…]`. The `--` separates options from pathspecs, allowing status to be limited to selected paths.
interview.followUp: What option gives a compact view? `--short` does; `--branch` can add branch and tracking information to that short output.

interview.question: How do you inspect more than file names?
interview.answer: The default is long format. `--verbose` additionally shows staged textual changes, while specifying it twice also shows unstaged working-tree changes.
interview.followUp: How can branch and stash context be added to concise output? Use `--branch` for branch/tracking information and `--show-stash` to show the number of stashed entries.

keyPoints: `git status` gives a summary of the repository's current working-tree state.
Changes between the staging index and HEAD represent content already staged for the next commit.
Changes between the working tree and index represent edits that are not yet staged.
Untracked files appear unless they match Git's ignore rules.
Use `--short` or `-s` for a concise two-column status representation.
Use `--porcelain` when another program must consume status output reliably.
Add `--branch` or `-b` to include branch and upstream tracking details with short output.
gotchas: Without an option, git status uses the long format, so scripts should request a stable machine-readable format explicitly.
For automation, prefer --porcelain because ordinary human-oriented output can vary with configuration or Git versions.

How Git works::.gitattributes.summary: `.gitattributes` assigns Git attributes to paths using pattern-based rules. It can control line-ending normalization, diff and merge behavior, filters, and whether paths appear in exported archives.
How Git works::.gitattributes.explanation: Git reads attribute rules from files such as .gitattributes and applies the matching attributes to paths. Each rule combines a pattern with one or more attributes, which can be enabled, disabled with a dash, or assigned a value; later matching rules override earlier ones. Built-in attributes control normalization, diffs, merges, filters, and archive export behavior.

example.title: A project .gitattributes file
example.code:
.gitattributes
*.txt text
*.png binary
*.md diff=markdown
*.generated merge=ours
export-ignore
example.explanation: This file makes text files follow Git's text handling, marks PNG files as binary, selects a Markdown diff driver, uses the ours merge driver for generated files, and excludes matching paths from archive exports.

useCases.scenario: Keep text files normalized consistently across platforms.

useCases.title: Path-specific diffs and merges
useCases.scenario: Choose specialized diff or merge behavior for selected file types.

useCases.title: Archive control
useCases.scenario: Exclude generated files or private metadata from `git archive` output.

keyPoints: A .gitattributes file associates per-path attributes with repository paths.
Each rule consists of a path pattern followed by attribute names or assignments.
Listing an attribute name enables it for matching paths.
Prefix an attribute with - to disable it.
The diff attribute controls whether and how Git presents differences for matching files.
The merge attribute selects file-level merge behavior during operations that need it.

How Git works::git archive.summary: Export the files represented by a named tree or commit as a tar, zip, or other supported archive. The result contains selected project files, not the repository's working metadata or history.
How Git works::git archive.explanation: Git archive takes a named tree or commit, packages its selected files in the requested archive format, and writes the result to standard output or a specified file. It packages the tree contents rather than the repository metadata, and optional paths restrict which files are included.

parameters.name: --format=<fmt>
parameters.description: Archive format, such as tar or zip; if omitted, Git can infer it from the output filename or use tar.

parameters.description: Destination file; without it, the archive is written to standard output.

parameters.name: <tree-ish>
parameters.description: Tree or commit to archive.

parameters.name: [<path>…]
parameters.description: Optional paths to include from the named tree.

How Git works::git archive.returns: Writes the archive to standard output unless --output specifies a file; with --remote, retrieves a tar archive from the remote repository.

example.title: Archive the current commit
example.code: git archive --format=tar --prefix=project/ -o project.tar HEAD
example.explanation: Creates a tar archive containing the files from the current commit, placing them under a project/ directory in the archive.

useCases.scenario: Create a distributable source snapshot for a release without including the repository directory.
