interview.question: What does git archive do?
interview.answer: It creates an archive containing the tree structure for a named tree and writes it to standard output. The archive format can be selected with --format, or redirected to a file with --output.
interview.followUp: How would you package only one directory? Provide that path after the tree-ish argument, because optional path arguments restrict the archived content.

interview.question: What is the role of tree-ish?
interview.answer: The required tree-ish identifies the tree or commit whose files are archived. If no path arguments follow it, all files and subdirectories in that tree are included.
interview.followUp: What happens if the target is a commit? Git archives the tree represented by that commit, not its repository history.

interview.question: How can you control the archive's layout and format?
interview.answer: Use --prefix to prepend a directory name to every archived path. Use --format to choose a supported format such as tar or zip, and --output to save the result to a file.
interview.followUp: How can a remote repository provide the archive? Supply --remote=<repo>; Git retrieves a tar archive through the remote archive service.

keyPoints: The archive preserves the selected tree's directory structure.
The documentation lists tar, zip, tar.gz, and tgz among the available format values.
Use --prefix to place archived paths beneath a common leading directory.
Use --output or -o to store the generated archive in a named file.
The --verbose option reports archive progress on standard error.
gotchas: When writing to a file, Git may infer the archive format from that file's name; otherwise the default is tar.
If --prefix is supplied more than once, the final prefix applies to tracked files.
Adding paths changes the selection; omitting them archives the complete named tree.

How Git works::git bundle.summary: Package selected Git objects and refs into one portable bundle file. Move it without a network connection, then verify and import its history into another repository.
How Git works::git bundle.explanation: Git bundle writes selected objects and references into a portable archive. After the file is moved by any offline method, another repository can verify its prerequisites and import the bundle with Git operations such as fetch, pull, or clone.
How Git works::git bundle.syntax:
git bundle create [-q | --quiet | --progress] [--version=<version>] <file> <git-rev-list-args>
git bundle verify [-q | --quiet] <file>
git bundle list-heads <file> [<refname>…]
git bundle unbundle [--progress] <file> [<refname>…]

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: Output bundle path for `create`, or input bundle path for other subcommands.

parameters.name: <git-rev-list-args>
parameters.description: Revision-selection arguments determining the commits and refs included in a created bundle.

parameters.name: [<refname>…]
parameters.description: Optional refs to restrict or inspect for `list-heads` and `unbundle`.

How Git works::git bundle.returns: Creates or reads a bundle file; `verify` reports validity and prerequisites, `list-heads` lists contained refs, and `unbundle` outputs the bundled objects for use by Git.

example.title: Create, verify, and fetch a bundle
example.code:
git bundle create repo.bundle main~3..main

git bundle verify repo.bundle
git fetch ../repo.bundle main:refs/remotes/bundle/main
example.explanation: Creates a bundle containing the selected commits, checks that the receiving repository has the required prerequisites, then imports the bundled branch into a remote-tracking ref.

useCases.title: Offline transfer
useCases.scenario: Two repositories must exchange commits while disconnected from a network.

useCases.title: Full or incremental backup
useCases.scenario: A repository needs a portable copy of all or part of its history.

useCases.title: Repository-state relay
useCases.scenario: One repository needs to pass its ref state to another repository.

interview.question: What problem does `git bundle` solve?
interview.answer: Use `git bundle create <file> <git-rev-list-args>` to package the selected history. The resulting file can be moved offline and then imported into another repository with Git operations such as fetch, pull, or clone.
interview.followUp: How can you determine whether a destination is prepared to receive it? Run `git bundle verify <file>`; it checks whether the bundle is valid and whether required prerequisite commits are available.

interview.question: How does a bundle represent Git history?
interview.answer: The `create` form selects the objects and refs described by its revision-list arguments and stores them in a bundle. The bundle has a header identifying the refs, followed by packed Git objects.
interview.followUp: Why must the revision arguments be chosen carefully? They define the history included, so omitting a needed range can leave the recipient without required objects.

interview.question: Which commands help inspect and validate a bundle?
interview.answer: `git bundle verify <file>` validates the bundle against the current repository and reports whether its prerequisites are present. `git bundle list-heads <file>` displays the refs recorded in the file, while `unbundle` extracts its objects.
interview.followUp: When would `list-heads` help? It lets you inspect available refs before deciding which bundled ref to import or fetch.

keyPoints: The command supports creating, unpacking, and inspecting Git bundle files.
Bundles transfer Git objects without requiring an active network server.
The same mechanism supports either incremental backups or complete repository backups.
A bundle can communicate the recorded ref state from one repository to another.

How Git works::git cherry.summary: Lists commits on one branch whose changes do or do not have equivalent patches on another branch. It compares patch content, so recreated commits can match even when their IDs differ.
How Git works::git cherry.explanation: Run git cherry to inspect whether commits on a working branch have equivalent changes in another branch. It compares the selected commit ranges by patch content rather than requiring identical commit IDs, so commits recreated by cherry-pick, am, or rebase can be recognized.

parameters.name: -v
parameters.description: Show commit subjects next to the SHA-1 values.

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: Branch to search for equivalent commits; defaults to HEAD's upstream branch.

parameters.name: <head>
parameters.description: Working branch to inspect; defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: <limit>
parameters.description: Exclude this commit and all earlier commits from the report.

How Git works::git cherry.returns: Prints each commit SHA-1 in <limit>..<head>, prefixed with '-' when an equivalent exists in <upstream> and '+' otherwise; -v also prints subjects.

example.title: Compare equivalent patches
example.code:
git init cherry-demo
cd cherry-demo
git config user.name Demo
git config user.email demo@example.com
echo base > file.txt
git add file.txt && git commit -m base
git branch upstream
echo change > file.txt
git commit -am change
git branch copied
# Inspect commits on HEAD relative to upstream
git cherry -v upstream HEAD
example.explanation: Creates a branch with one change and compares the current branch with its upstream counterpart; the output marks equivalent patches with '-' and unmatched patches with '+'.

useCases.title: Detect already-applied patches
useCases.scenario: Check whether a topic branch's patches have already landed upstream.

useCases.title: Find outstanding work
useCases.scenario: Review which commits on the current branch still need to be sent or applied.

useCases.title: Validate copied commits
useCases.scenario: Verify the result of cherry-picking, rebasing, or applying patches.

keyPoints: The command reports the object ID of each commit in the selected limit..head range.
A minus sign means an equivalent patch exists upstream; a plus sign means no equivalent was found there.
It can identify changes recreated through cherry-pick, applying patches, or rebasing even when the resulting commit IDs differ.
Use -v to include each reported commit's subject beside its object ID.
The upstream argument names the branch whose commits are checked for equivalent changes.
The head argument identifies the branch whose commits are examined and defaults to the current HEAD.
A common use is checking whether a patch series has already been applied by an upstream maintainer.
gotchas: Equivalence is determined from the diff after whitespace and line-number differences are removed; visually or semantically similar changes that produce different diffs may not match.
If you omit the upstream argument, Git uses HEAD's configured upstream branch, which may not be the branch you intended to compare.
When a limit is supplied, that commit and every earlier commit are excluded from the report.

How Git works::git fsck.summary: Verifies the connectivity and validity of Git’s object database. It can also list objects that are unreachable from the selected or default reachability heads.
How Git works::git fsck.explanation: Git walks the object database from selected head nodes, normally the index, refs, and reflogs, while checking object validity and connectivity. It reports corruption such as missing or invalid objects; with --unreachable, it also reports existing objects that no specified head can reach.

parameters.name: <object>…
parameters.description: Optional object to use as the head of an unreachability trace; if omitted, the documented default heads are used.

How Git works::git fsck.returns: Reports object connectivity and validity problems, plus optional root, tag, dangling, or unreachable objects; it does not return a documented data value.

example.title: Check integrity and find unreachable objects
example.code: git fsck --full --unreachable
example.explanation: Checks the repository's object database and reports objects that are not reachable from the command's default heads.

useCases.title: Detect missing or malformed objects
useCases.scenario: Repository maintenance

useCases.title: Locate unreachable commits and other objects
useCases.scenario: History recovery

useCases.title: Trace reachability from specified objects
useCases.scenario: Targeted graph analysis

useCases.title: Check tag, commit, and tree connectivity only
useCases.scenario: Fast connectivity checks

interview.question: What does git fsck check?
interview.answer: It verifies object connectivity and validity, including general object sanity, and reports corruption such as missing or bad objects. With --unreachable, it also lists objects not reachable from the chosen or default heads.
interview.followUp: How can you search for commits removed from refs but retained by reflogs? Use --no-reflogs so reflog-only commits are not treated as reachable.

interview.question: What are the default heads for reachability analysis?
interview.answer: Without explicit objects, Git uses the index, SHA-1 references in the refs namespace, and reflogs as heads, unless --no-reflogs is supplied. Reachability is evaluated by tracing from those heads.
interview.followUp: How can the index be included explicitly as a reachability head? Use --cache, which treats indexed objects as head nodes.

interview.question: How do --unreachable and --connectivity-only differ?
interview.answer: --unreachable prints existing objects that cannot be reached from any reference node or other specified head. --connectivity-only instead limits checking to connectivity among tags, commits, and tree objects.
interview.followUp: What does --strict add? It enables stricter checking of object contents and metadata beyond ordinary checks.

keyPoints: The command checks both whether objects are valid and whether the object graph is connected from its heads.
Integrity failures are surfaced as reported corruption, including missing or malformed objects.
With --unreachable, it lists existing objects outside the reachability graph of the selected heads.
Passing an object supplies a custom starting point for the reachability analysis.
The --root option identifies objects that have no incoming references in the examined graph.
The --cache option makes indexed objects additional reachability roots.
gotchas: Use --no-reflogs when looking specifically for commits that disappeared from refs but remain in reflogs.
--connectivity-only skips the broader object-sanity checks, so it is not a complete integrity check.
Dangling objects are reported by default; use --no-dangling if that output is not wanted.

How Git works::git gc and git maintenanc.summary: git maintenance runs repository-optimization tasks, including gc, which cleans unnecessary data and optimizes the local repository. Prefer the task-oriented command `git maintenance run --task=gc` when possible.
How Git works::git gc and git maintenanc.explanation: Git maintenance organizes repository housekeeping into tasks. Its gc task cleans unnecessary files and optimizes repository data; it can repack objects into one pack-file and remove stale data, while the maintenance command also supports scheduling and other task-oriented workflows.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling the maintenance run, including one or more task selections.

How Git works::git gc and git maintenanc.returns: Runs the requested maintenance tasks; the page does not specify a separate return value.

example.title: Run garbage-collection maintenance
example.code: git maintenance run --task=gc
example.explanation: Runs Git's garbage-collection maintenance task in the current repository.

useCases.title: Clean and optimize a local repository
useCases.scenario: A repository has accumulated unnecessary files or inefficient object storage.

useCases.title: Run selected tasks in order
useCases.scenario: A script needs deterministic housekeeping rather than the default strategy.

useCases.title: Manage scheduled maintenance
useCases.scenario: A team wants recurring repository optimization with Git's maintenance framework.

interview.question: What does the gc task do?
interview.answer: The gc maintenance task cleans unnecessary files and optimizes the local repository. It is one task within the broader git maintenance command, whose purpose is to speed up Git commands and reduce repository storage.
interview.followUp: Why might gc be expensive? It can repack all Git objects into a single pack-file, especially affecting large repositories.

interview.question: How do you run only garbage-collection maintenance?
interview.answer: git maintenance run executes maintenance tasks, and --task=gc selects garbage collection explicitly. Supplying task options runs the selected tasks in the specified order.
interview.followUp: What happens without an explicit task? The documented default strategy for manual maintenance is gc.

interview.question: How does git maintenance relate to git gc?
interview.answer: Git maintenance is broader than gc: it provides task-oriented optimization plus commands for starting, stopping, registering, unregistering, and checking whether maintenance is needed. The gc task is specifically the cleanup and optimization task.
interview.followUp: Why use maintenance rather than git gc? The documentation recommends git maintenance run --task=gc when possible.

keyPoints: Maintenance improves repository operation by optimizing stored data, which can make other Git commands faster and reduce storage needs.
The run subcommand can execute one or several maintenance tasks.
Multiple explicitly selected tasks execute sequentially in the order supplied.
The gc task removes unneeded repository files while optimizing the local repository.
The name gc refers to garbage collection, although the task is a collection of several housekeeping operations.
Manual maintenance uses the gc strategy by default when no other strategy is selected.
gotchas: The gc task may be costly on large repositories because it repacks every Git object into one pack-file.
Running gc can remove stale data, so avoid treating it as a risk-free operation during sensitive repository work.
The documentation recommends the maintenance form instead of invoking git gc directly when possible.

How Git works::Git hooks.summary: Git hooks are executable programs that Git runs at defined lifecycle points, such as before a commit. They normally live in $GIT_DIR/hooks, or in the directory selected by core.hooksPath.
How Git works::Git hooks.explanation: Git hooks are executable programs stored in a repository’s hooks directory and invoked at defined points in Git’s execution. Git normally looks in $GIT_DIR/hooks, unless core.hooksPath changes the location; hooks receive context through arguments, environment variables, or standard input, and Git sets their working directory according to repository type and hook category.
How Git works::Git hooks.returns: Hook-specific process exit status; a failing hook can prevent the associated Git operation.

example.title: Reject commits with whitespace errors
example.code:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
if git diff --cached --check; then
  exit 0
fi
exit 1
example.explanation: Save this executable file as .git/hooks/pre-commit. Git runs it before creating a commit; a nonzero exit status rejects the commit.

useCases.title: Client-side validation
useCases.scenario: Run formatting, linting, or tests before a commit is created.

useCases.title: Server-side policy enforcement
useCases.scenario: Enforce repository-side checks when updates arrive.

useCases.title: Post-operation automation
useCases.scenario: Trigger notifications or cleanup after Git completes an operation.

interview.question: Where does Git look for hooks, and how can that location change?
interview.answer: Git searches for executable hook programs in $GIT_DIR/hooks by default. The core.hooksPath configuration variable can redirect that lookup to another directory.
interview.followUp: How can a hook receive inputs? It can use command-line arguments, environment variables, and standard input.

interview.question: How does the pre-commit hook affect git commit?
interview.answer: The pre-commit hook runs during git commit before Git obtains the proposed commit message and creates the commit. It takes no parameters and can be bypassed with --no-verify.
interview.followUp: What determines whether it blocks the commit? Its process result: a hook can run validation and return a failure status to stop the operation.

interview.question: What working directory should a hook expect?
interview.answer: Git changes the hook’s working directory before invocation. For a non-bare repository this is normally the working-tree root, while for a bare repository it is $GIT_DIR.
interview.followUp: What is the push-hook exception? pre-receive, update, post-receive, post-update, and push-to-checkout always execute in $GIT_DIR.

keyPoints: A hook is a program that Git invokes at a defined lifecycle point.
The default per-repository hook directory is $GIT_DIR/hooks.
core.hooksPath lets you use a different hook directory.
Hook inputs may come from the environment, command-line arguments, or standard input.
The pre-commit hook is invoked by git commit.
pre-commit receives no parameters and runs before Git gets the message and creates the commit.
gotchas: A hook file must be executable or Git ignores it.
Some client-side checks, including pre-commit, can be skipped with --no-verify.
Push-related hooks run from $GIT_DIR even when the repository is non-bare.

How Git works::git sparse-checkout.summary: Use git sparse-checkout to materialize only part of a repository’s tracked tree while retaining the full repository history. Select directories with cone mode or patterns with non-cone mode.
How Git works::git sparse-checkout.explanation: Sparse checkout changes the working tree so only a selected subset of tracked files is present; the rest remain tracked and represented in the index with the skip-worktree bit. The subset can be specified as directories in cone mode or patterns in non-cone mode. Git stores the selection and updates the working tree when you set, add, reapply, or disable the configuration.
How Git works::git sparse-checkout.syntax: git sparse-checkout (init | list | set | add | reapply | disable | check-rules | clean) [<options>]

parameters.name: subcommand and options
parameters.description: One of init, list, set, add, reapply, disable, check-rules, or clean, followed by subcommand-specific options and paths or patterns.

How Git works::git sparse-checkout.returns: Updates the sparse-checkout configuration and working tree; list and check-rules report information, while disable restores all tracked files.

example.title: Select directory trees
example.code:
git clone --no-checkout https://example.com/repo.git repo
cd repo
git sparse-checkout set --cone src docs
git sparse-checkout list
example.explanation: Clones repository history without populating every file, then keeps only the src and docs directory trees in the working tree.

useCases.title: Work on one part of a monorepo
useCases.scenario: A monorepo contains independent applications and libraries, but a developer needs only one directory tree locally.

useCases.title: Reduce working-tree footprint
useCases.scenario: A build or analysis task needs a focused set of paths without populating unrelated tracked files.

useCases.title: Change the selected tree
useCases.scenario: A developer needs to switch the locally materialized subset as their task changes.

interview.question: What does sparse checkout change?
interview.answer: It reduces the working tree to a subset of tracked files while leaving the rest tracked. Git uses the skip-worktree bit in the index to mark files that should not be present locally.
interview.followUp: How would you restore the complete working tree? Run git sparse-checkout disable, which turns off core.sparseCheckout and restores all files.

interview.question: What is the difference between cone and non-cone mode?
interview.answer: Cone mode is the default and accepts directory names, making common directory-based selections straightforward. Non-cone mode accepts patterns, which supports more precise selections.
interview.followUp: When would non-cone mode be preferable? Use it when the desired subset cannot be expressed cleanly as directory-based cone patterns.

interview.question: Which subcommands change or inspect the selection?
interview.answer: Use git sparse-checkout set to enable the needed configuration, write the requested selection, and update the working tree. Use add to extend the current directory or pattern selection, and reapply to enforce the existing rules again.
interview.followUp: What command shows the active selection? git sparse-checkout list displays the configured sparse-checkout entries.

keyPoints: Sparse checkout limits the files materialized in the working tree without changing which files are tracked.
The same command can replace the selected subset or return the working copy to its full tracked-file state.
Choose directory-based cone mode for standard tree selections, or pattern-based non-cone mode for custom matching.
The set operation enables or adjusts the relevant sparse-checkout configuration before applying the selection.
The add subcommand expands the current selection with directories or patterns, according to the active mode.
The reapply subcommand makes the working tree conform again to the current sparse rules.
gotchas: Cone mode expects directories rather than arbitrary file patterns; use non-cone mode when the selection needs pattern-level precision.
Disabling sparse checkout repopulates the working tree with all tracked files; it does not remove repository history.

How Git works::git worktree.summary: Git worktree lets one repository host multiple working directories, so different branches can be checked out and worked on at the same time. Each linked worktree lives in its own folder while sharing repository data.
How Git works::git worktree.explanation: Git keeps multiple working directories attached to one repository. Adding a worktree creates a separate checkout at the requested path, with its own branch state and per-worktree files while repository data is shared; list, lock, move, prune, remove, and unlock manage those linked directories.

parameters.description: Destination directory for the new worktree.

parameters.name: [<commit-ish>]
parameters.description: Optional branch, tag, or commit to check out.

git worktree add -b feature/login ../login-worktree main

interview.question: What problem does git worktree solve?
interview.answer: `git worktree` attaches multiple working trees to one repository, so more than one branch can be checked out concurrently. Each linked worktree has its own checkout-related state while sharing the repository’s common data.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent cleanup from deleting metadata for an offline worktree? Lock it with `git worktree lock`, optionally recording a reason.

interview.question: How do you create a worktree for a feature branch?
interview.answer: `git worktree add <path> <commit-ish>` creates a linked worktree at the path and checks out the chosen commit or branch there. Using `-b <new-branch>` creates and checks out a new branch for that worktree.
interview.followUp: How can you create a worktree without switching to a branch? Use `--detach` and provide the desired commit-ish.

interview.question: How are worktrees inspected and cleaned up?
interview.answer: Use `git worktree list` to inspect registered worktrees, and `git worktree remove <worktree>` when a linked worktree is no longer needed. If its directory was removed outside Git, `git worktree prune` cleans stale administrative data.
interview.followUp: What if the worktree path moved? Use `git worktree move <worktree> <new-path>` or `git worktree repair` when the working tree’s administrative link needs correction.

Different branches can be active simultaneously because each worktree has its own checkout.
The `add` subcommand creates and registers another working directory under the repository.
The path identifies the new directory, while the optional commit-ish selects the starting branch or commit.
Git treats the directory and its associated administrative metadata as one managed worktree.
Remove an obsolete linked worktree through Git rather than leaving its registration behind.

How Git works::Objects, refs and the DAG.explanation: Git stores project history in an object database. Commits point to trees, trees organize blobs and other trees, and parent links connect commits into history; refs name interesting objects or other refs, while HEAD identifies the checked-out branch.

git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD^{tree}
git cat-file -t HEAD:greeting.txt

interview.question: What are Git’s core object types and how are they related?
interview.answer: Git’s object database has three main object types described here: blobs store file data, trees point to blobs and other trees, and commits reference one tree plus parent commits. Together, these links represent snapshots and their history.
interview.followUp: How does a directory snapshot get represented? A tree records entries that point to blobs for files and to other trees for subdirectories.

interview.question: How does Git represent project history as a graph?
interview.answer: A commit represents one project-history step and references a tree describing its contents. Its parent references identify immediately preceding commits, so commits form a history graph rather than a simple list.
interview.followUp: Why can the graph branch? A commit may have more than one parent, which represents a merge of histories.

interview.question: What is a ref, and what roles do branches, tags, and HEAD play?
interview.answer: Refs are named pointers to interesting points in history. Branch refs identify the latest commit of a branch, tag refs identify tagged objects, and HEAD identifies the currently checked-out branch.
interview.followUp: What does HEAD resolve to? It names the current branch ref, which in turn identifies the branch’s latest commit.

keyPoints: Blobs are the objects that contain file contents.
Trees describe directories by linking to file blobs and nested directory trees.
Each commit points to one root tree and zero or more parent commits.
A commit records one versioned step in the project’s history.
Parent links connect a commit to its immediately preceding history.
Refs provide names for significant locations in the object history.
Branch refs store the object name of the branch’s latest commit.
Tag refs are stored beneath the ref/tags namespace.
gotchas: A ref is not limited to directly naming an object; it can point through another ref.
HEAD normally names a branch rather than directly naming the current commit.

The signature is embedded in the commit, and git verify-commit can check it later.

git config --global user.signingkey ABC123
git commit -S -m "Add feature"
git verify-commit HEAD
example.explanation: Configures the signing key, creates a signed commit, then verifies the signature.

Inspecting history::git bisect.summary: Find the commit that introduced a bug by binary-searching between known-good and known-bad revisions. Classify each checked-out midpoint until Git isolates the first bad commit.
Inspecting history::git bisect.explanation: Git bisect narrows a known-good to known-bad revision range by repeatedly checking out a midpoint. You test that revision and mark it good or bad; Git uses the result to halve the remaining range until it identifies the commit that introduced the change, after which you reset the bisect session.

parameters.name: <subcommand> <options>
parameters.description: Subcommand and its options, such as start, good, bad, skip, run, or reset.

Inspecting history::git bisect.returns: The command identifies the first commit that introduced the change and reports it; reset exits the bisect state.

example.title: Find the first bad commit
example.code:
git bisect start
 git bisect bad HEAD
 git bisect good v1.0.0
# Test the checked-out commit, then mark it:
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad
# Repeat until Git identifies the first bad commit
git bisect reset
example.explanation: Start with known bad and good revisions, classify each checked-out midpoint, then leave bisect mode after the culprit is found.

useCases.title: Locate a regression
useCases.scenario: A regression appears somewhere between a release and the current branch.

useCases.title: Automate historical testing
useCases.scenario: A test or diagnostic command can classify every checked-out revision.

useCases.scenario: Some historical revisions fail to build or cannot reproduce the issue.

interview.question: How does git bisect locate a bug-introducing commit?
interview.answer: It performs a binary search over revision history. You provide a known bad revision and one or more known good revisions, then classify the revisions Git selects until the first bad commit is found.
interview.followUp: What if a midpoint cannot be tested? Use git bisect skip for that revision or range; Git may then report multiple possible commits if the result cannot be uniquely determined.

interview.question: What conditions must the starting revisions satisfy?
interview.answer: A good revision must be known to be before the bug was introduced, while a bad revision contains the bug. Each classification tells Git which half of the remaining history to discard.
interview.followUp: Can the labels be changed? Yes: start can define alternative old/new terms, and the corresponding classification commands can use those terms.

interview.question: How do you finish and leave a bisect session?
interview.answer: The bisect session changes the checked-out revision while it searches. After the culprit is identified, git bisect reset ends the session and returns to the original HEAD.
interview.followUp: How can repeated testing be automated? The documentation provides git bisect run, which runs a command at each revision and uses its exit status to classify it.

keyPoints: Git bisect searches commit history efficiently by repeatedly halving the candidate range.
Begin by identifying a revision where the defect is reproducible and mark it bad.
Also provide a revision that predates the defect and is verified to work.
Git checks out an intermediate commit for you to evaluate.
Continue classifying revisions until the search isolates the introducing commit.
Use skip when particular revisions or ranges cannot be evaluated.

Inspecting history::git blame.sourceTitle: git-blame - Show what revision and author last modified each line of a file
Inspecting history::git blame.summary: Show which revision and author last modified each line of a file. It can narrow the analysis to selected lines and follow code across renames, moves, or copies.
Inspecting history::git blame.explanation: Git examines the specified file in the current revision by default and annotates each line with the revision that last modified it. You can provide another starting revision, limit the output with -L, and use -M or -C to investigate lines moved or copied within or between files.

parameters.name: <rev>
parameters.description: Optional starting revision; without it, the current file revision is used.

parameters.name: -L <range>
parameters.description: Restricts annotation to a requested line range; may be specified repeatedly.

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: File whose lines are annotated.

Inspecting history::git blame.returns: Annotated output for the specified file, including line content and information about the revision and author associated with each line.

example.title: Inspect a selected line range
example.code: git blame -L 10,20 -- README.md
example.explanation: Annotates lines 10 through 20 of README.md with the commit and author associated with each line.

useCases.scenario: Investigating when and by whom a particular implementation line was introduced.

useCases.title: Limit history to a range
useCases.scenario: Reviewing only a suspicious section of a large source file.

useCases.title: Track moved or copied code
useCases.scenario: Following code after refactoring or extraction into another file.

interview.question: What does git blame show?
interview.answer: By default, git blame annotates each line in the given file using the revision that last modified that line. Its output identifies the relevant revision and author, and an optional revision can be supplied as the starting point.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect only part of a file? Use -L with a line range; it may be supplied more than once and ranges can overlap.

interview.question: How does blame handle moved or copied code?
interview.answer: Use -M to follow lines moved within a file and -C to follow lines copied or moved from another file. Whole-file renames are followed automatically.
interview.followUp: What limitation remains? Blame still does not report lines that were deleted or replaced; inspect diffs or use pickaxe history searches for those.

interview.question: What is the purpose of --reverse?
interview.answer: The --reverse form walks history forward rather than backward. It reports the last revision in which a line existed, rather than the revision in which the line appeared.
interview.followUp: How can the analysis be narrowed while using history? Supply -L to restrict annotation to selected lines.

keyPoints: Each output line is associated with the revision that most recently modified it.
A revision argument changes the point in history from which annotation begins.
Use -L to inspect one or more selected line ranges instead of the whole file.
Whole-file renames are tracked automatically while attributing line history.
Use -M and -C when attribution should follow code moved within a file or copied between files.
The --reverse option analyzes line existence by traversing history from earlier to later revisions.
gotchas: Deleted or replaced lines are not represented in the report; use git diff or pickaxe-style history searches for those changes.

Inspecting history::git describe.sourceTitle: git-describe - Give an object a human readable name based on an available ref
Inspecting history::git describe.summary: Names a commit using the nearest reachable tag. It is useful for generating build and version strings, and can mark a dirty working tree.
Inspecting history::git describe.explanation: Git selects a reachable tag for the target commit and formats the result as the tag alone when it points directly to that commit, or as the tag plus the number of commits after it and an abbreviated commit ID. With no commit argument, the target is HEAD; --dirty additionally marks a modified working tree.
Inspecting history::git describe.syntax:
git describe [--all] [--tags] [--contains] [--abbrev=<n>] [<commit-ish>…]
git describe [--all] [--tags] [--contains] [--abbrev=<n>] --dirty[=<mark>]
git describe <blob>

parameters.name: --all
parameters.description: Consider all refs under refs/.

parameters.name: --tags
parameters.description: Consider tags in refs/tags, including lightweight tags.

parameters.name: --contains
parameters.description: Find a tag that comes after and contains the commit.

parameters.name: --abbrev=<n>
parameters.description: Use at least n hexadecimal digits for the abbreviated object name, extending as needed for uniqueness.

parameters.name: --dirty[=<mark>]
parameters.description: Describe the working tree and append mark when it is dirty.

parameters.name: <commit-ish>…
parameters.description: Commit-ish object name(s) to describe; omitted means HEAD.

Inspecting history::git describe.returns: A human-readable object name based on a reachable ref, typically a tag followed by a commit count and abbreviated object name when needed.

example.title: Describe the current checkout
example.code: git describe --tags --dirty
example.explanation: Print a version-like name for the current commit and append a dirty marker when tracked worktree changes are present.

useCases.scenario: Generate package, binary, or container version text from repository history.

useCases.title: Release identification
useCases.scenario: Display a concise human-readable identity for a release candidate or deployment.

useCases.title: Dirty-tree labeling
useCases.scenario: Detect whether the checked-out working tree contains uncommitted changes.

interview.question: How does git describe construct its normal output?
interview.answer: It finds the most recent reachable tag. If that tag names the commit directly, only the tag is printed; otherwise the output includes the number of commits since the tag and an abbreviated object name.
interview.followUp: How would you include lightweight tags? Use --tags; --all is broader and permits any ref in the refs namespace.

interview.question: What does git describe target by default, and what does --dirty do?
interview.answer: With no commit-ish argument, Git describes HEAD. The argument can identify one or more commits or another supported object, while --dirty applies the description to the working tree.
interview.followUp: What does --dirty add? It appends the specified mark, or -dirty by default, when the working tree is dirty.

interview.question: Which options change the reference search?
interview.answer: By default, the search uses annotated tags reachable from the commit. --tags includes tags in refs/tags, --all considers refs in refs/, and --contains searches for a later tag that contains the commit.
interview.followUp: How can output length be controlled? --abbrev=<n> requests at least n hexadecimal digits, with more used when needed for uniqueness.

keyPoints: A commit exactly named by its selected tag produces only that tag in the output.
When the commit is newer than its tag, Git reports how many commits separate them.
The non-tag portion ends with an abbreviated object name for the described commit.
Pass commit-ish names to describe a particular commit instead of relying on the default target.
Use --tags when lightweight tags should participate in tag selection.
Use --all to broaden selection beyond tags to refs under refs/.
The default abbreviation is seven hexadecimal digits; --abbrev=<n> lets you request a different minimum.
gotchas: The default search considers annotated tags; use --tags to include lightweight tags, or --all to consider any ref in refs/.
--dirty describes the working tree and adds its mark only when the working tree differs from HEAD.
--contains changes the search to a tag that contains the commit, rather than a tag reachable before it.

Inspecting history::git diff --staged.summary: Show the staged changes that the next commit would contain by comparing the index with HEAD. It is an alias-equivalent spelling of git diff --cached.
Inspecting history::git diff --staged.explanation: The command compares the index with a commit, defaulting to HEAD when no commit is supplied. It prints staged modifications, additions, and deletions; optional paths restrict the comparison, while worktree-only edits are not included.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Diff formatting and comparison options.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: Commit or tree to compare against; defaults to HEAD.

parameters.name: [--] [<path>...]
parameters.description: Optional path separator and paths limiting the diff.

Inspecting history::git diff --staged.returns: A textual diff of index changes relative to the selected commit or tree.

example.title: Inspect staged content
example.code:
git init demo
cd demo
printf 'one\n' > file.txt
git add file.txt
git diff --staged
example.explanation: Stages a file and prints the index-versus-HEAD patch that the next commit would contain.

interview.question: What does git diff --staged show?
interview.answer: It compares the index, also called the staging area, with HEAD and shows the patch prepared for the next commit. Changes that exist only in the working tree are excluded.
interview.followUp: How can the comparison target be changed? Supply a commit after the option, such as git diff --staged HEAD~1, to compare the index with that commit.

interview.question: What is the default comparison target?
interview.answer: The command defaults the comparison commit to HEAD when no commit is provided. This makes it a practical preview of the next commit’s content.
interview.followUp: What happens on an unborn branch? With no commit argument, all staged changes are shown because HEAD does not exist.

interview.question: How does --staged relate to --cached?
interview.answer: git diff --staged and git diff --cached are equivalent because --staged is an alias for --cached. Both inspect changes staged in the index relative to the selected commit.
interview.followUp: How can you limit the output? Add -- followed by one or more paths to restrict the displayed changes.

keyPoints: It previews the changes currently staged for the next commit.
Without an explicit commit, the index is compared with HEAD.
The command belongs to git diff’s modes for comparing the index with a tree.
With --merge-base, the comparison uses the merge base of the supplied commit and HEAD.
gotchas: In a repository without a HEAD commit, the command displays all staged changes instead of comparing against HEAD.
The equivalent spelling is git diff --cached.

Inspecting history::git log --graph.summary: `git log --graph` adds an ASCII representation of commit relationships beside the commit log. It can insert connector-only lines and uses topological ordering by default.
Inspecting history::git log --graph.explanation: `git log --graph` prints a text-based representation of commit relationships on the left side of the normal log output. It can add lines between commits to draw the structure, and it changes traversal behavior by enabling parent rewriting and implying topological ordering unless date ordering is explicitly selected.

parameters.description: Options controlling formatting, ordering, traversal, and other log behavior; include `--graph`.

parameters.name: <revision-range>
parameters.description: A commit, ref, or revision expression that selects the commits to inspect.

parameters.name: <path>…
parameters.description: One or more paths after `--` to limit the history to changes affecting those paths.

interview.question: What does `git log --graph` do?
interview.answer: It draws a text-based graphical representation of commit history on the left side of the log output. Extra lines may appear between commits so the graph can be drawn correctly.
interview.followUp: What ordering does it imply? It implies `--topo-order` by default, although `--date-order` may also be specified.

interview.question: What is the syntax for using `--graph` with `git log`?
interview.answer: The command is `git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>…]`, with `--graph` supplied as an option. For example, `git log --graph --oneline` combines graph rendering with compact commit formatting.
interview.followUp: How would you restrict the displayed history? Add a revision range or path, such as `git log --graph main..feature -- src/`.

interview.question: What limitations or traversal effects should you know?
interview.answer: `--graph` cannot be combined with `--no-walk`. The option also enables parent rewriting, which affects history simplification while Git traverses commits.
interview.followUp: Why might the output contain extra graph-only lines? Git inserts them between commits to represent the graph history properly.

keyPoints: The graph appears to the left of the ordinary commit-log information.
Graph connectors can create lines that contain no separate commit entry.
`git log` remains the underlying command: it lists commits, while `--graph` changes their presentation.
Unless another ordering option is selected, commits are shown newest first.
gotchas: Do not combine `--graph` with `--no-walk`; the documentation marks that combination as unsupported.
The default traversal favors topology, while `--date-order` can be requested when date constraints should also influence the display.

Inspecting history::git notes.summary: Attach or inspect metadata associated with a commit without modifying the commit object or its hash. Notes are separate Git references and are commonly used to supplement commit messages.
Inspecting history::git notes.explanation: Git notes are separate annotations associated with Git objects, commonly commits. Adding or reading one does not modify the annotated object, so the commit hash remains unchanged; by default, notes are stored under refs/notes/commits and can be viewed with log or show.
Inspecting history::git notes.syntax:
git notes [list [<object>]]
git notes add [-f] [--allow-empty] [--[no-]separator | --separator=<paragraph-break>] [--[no-]stripspace] [-F <file> | -m <msg> | (-c | -C) <object>] [-e] [<object>]
git notes edit [--allow-empty] [<object>]
git notes show [<object>]
git notes merge [-v | -q] [-s <strategy>] <notes-ref>

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: Optional object whose note is operated on; commonly a commit.

parameters.name: <msg>
parameters.description: Inline note text supplied to the add operation.

parameters.name: <notes-ref>
parameters.description: Notes reference used by merge operations or configured display/storage behavior.

Inspecting history::git notes.returns: The command updates or reads a note associated with a Git object; the annotated object itself is not changed.

example.title: Attach and inspect a commit note
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
echo hello > file.txt
git add file.txt && git commit -m "Initial commit"
commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git notes add -m "Reviewed by CI" "$commit"
git notes show "$commit"
git show "$commit"
example.explanation: Creates a commit, attaches a note to it, displays the note directly, and then shows the commit with its note.

interview.question: What problem does git notes solve?
interview.answer: git notes attaches a note to an object without changing the object. For commits, this lets you add supplemental information while preserving the original commit hash.
interview.followUp: How are notes stored? They are normally kept under the separate refs/notes/commits reference rather than inside the commit object.

interview.question: How do you add and inspect a note?
interview.answer: The basic form is git notes add, optionally followed by -m for an inline message and an object name. If no object is supplied, Git uses the default object in the relevant context.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect the result? Use git notes show <object>, or use git log or git show to display notes with the commit.

interview.question: Does changing a note change a commit?
interview.answer: The command supports adding, removing, and reading notes attached to Git objects. Notes are kept separately, so changing a note does not rewrite the annotated object.
interview.followUp: Can notes be used beyond commits? Yes. The documentation describes them as object notes, although supplementing commit messages is the typical use.

Use notes to record review results, test metadata, or other context after a commit already exists.
The default notes reference is refs/notes/commits.
History output can present a commit's note together with its original message.
git notes add creates or replaces a note, with options for forced replacement and empty notes.
git notes show reads the note associated with the specified object.
gotchas: Notes use refs/notes/commits by default, but another notes reference can be selected through Git configuration or related options.
A note is separate metadata; it is not automatically part of the commit message itself, even though standard history views can display it alongside that message.

Inspecting history::git range-diff.summary: Compare two versions of a patch series or two commit ranges. Git pairs corresponding commits and shows how their patches, messages, and metadata differ.
Inspecting history::git range-diff.explanation: Git first forms the two commit ranges, then matches commits whose patches are sufficiently similar. interview.question: What does `git range-diff` compare?
interview.answer: It compares two patch series or, more generally, two commit ranges. Git pairs commits whose patch-level differences are reasonably small, then displays changes between the paired commits.
interview.followUp: How can you compare a range before and after a rebase? Use the same base for both ranges, such as `git range-diff origin/main..old-tip origin/main..new-tip`.

interview.question: How can commit ranges be specified?
interview.answer: You can provide two ranges directly, use a symmetric three-dot form, or provide one base followed by two revisions. The three-dot form expands to the two base-relative ranges.
interview.followUp: Why prefer an explicit base in automation? It makes the intended common starting point clear and avoids relying on an implicitly selected merge base.

interview.question: How are merge commits handled?
interview.answer: By default, merge commits are excluded. The `--diff-merges=<format>` option asks Git to generate merge diffs using the corresponding `git log` format and include them.
interview.followUp: What other output controls are available? The command also supports options such as `--left-only`, `--right-only`, `--creation-factor`, and `--remerge-diff`.

keyPoints: Use it to review how a patch series changed between iterations, including after rebasing or revising commits.
The comparison starts by matching related commits across the two supplied ranges.
Patch correspondence considers author information, the commit message, and the commit diff.
A two-range invocation accepts ordinary base-to-revision ranges as well as single-commit and mainline-parent forms.
The symmetric `rev1...rev2` form compares each revision against the other revision's side.
The three-argument form compares two revisions using one shared base.
Use `--diff-merges=<format>` when merge commits must participate in the comparison.
gotchas: Merge commits are ignored unless you request merge diffs with the relevant diff-merges option.
Commit pairing is heuristic: author data, messages, and patch diffs all contribute to whether commits correspond.

Inspecting history::git shortlog.summary: Group selected commits by author and title for release summaries. Choose between detailed subjects, per-author counts, email addresses, contribution ranking, and custom Git log formats.

interview.question: What does git shortlog do?
interview.answer: It summarizes log output by grouping commits by author and title. The default output is suitable for release announcements.
interview.followUp: How would you produce only contribution counts? Use --summary or -s, optionally with --numbered to rank authors by commit count.

interview.question: How do you restrict and enrich its output?
interview.answer: Use a revision range after the options, such as v1.0.0..HEAD, to limit the commits considered. A path can be supplied after -- to restrict the history to that path.
interview.followUp: How can you include contact information? Add --email or -e to show each author’s email address.

interview.question: How can commit descriptions be customized?
interview.answer: The --format option replaces the default commit subject with another description format. Its value can be any format accepted by git log’s --format option.
interview.followUp: Can shortlog process piped log data? Yes: git log --pretty=short | git shortlog [options] supplies formatted log output through standard input.

keyPoints: Use shortlog to turn commit history into a compact contributor-oriented release summary.
The output groups every selected commit under its author and displays its title.
--numbered ranks authors by how many selected commits they have rather than alphabetically.
Use -s or --summary when you need one count per author without commit subjects.
Use -e or --email to add each author’s email address to the author listing.
--format accepts git log formatting so each grouped entry can show fields other than the subject.
gotchas: Without a revision range, non-interactive input or a repository without a current branch can make shortlog summarize log data read from standard input rather than the expected repository history.
Patch markers are removed from commit descriptions, so output may not preserve the original subject exactly.

Inspecting history::git show.summary: Print one or more Git objects. For commits, git show displays the commit message and textual diff; other object types receive type-specific output.
Inspecting history::git show.explanation: Run git show with an object name such as HEAD, a tag, or a commit ID. Git resolves the object and prints information according to its type: a commit includes its message and textual diff, while tags, trees, and blobs produce their corresponding object content or listing.

parameters.name: [options]
