parameters.name: [object]…
parameters.description: One or more Git object expressions, such as a commit, tag, tree, blob, or historical path expression.

Inspecting history::git show.returns: Writes the selected object's representation to standard output: commit message and diff, tag message and referenced objects, tree names, or blob contents.

example.title: Inspect the current commit
example.code: git show --stat --oneline HEAD
example.explanation: Displays the current commit's abbreviated identity, subject, and changed-file summary.

useCases.title: Inspect a commit and its patch
useCases.scenario: Review a recent change before merging or debugging.

useCases.title: Retrieve historical file contents
useCases.scenario: Read a file exactly as it existed in an earlier revision.

useCases.title: Inspect annotated tags
useCases.scenario: Check a release tag and the object it names.

useCases.title: Restrict commit output
useCases.scenario: Get a concise subject or summary instead of the full patch.

interview.question: What does git show display?
interview.answer: git show displays one or more Git objects. For commits, it prints the log message and textual diff; tags, trees, and blobs are shown according to their object type.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect only a commit subject? Use `git show -s --format=%s <commit>`.

interview.question: Which kinds of objects can git show inspect?
interview.answer: The object argument can identify different Git object types, including commits, tags, trees, and blobs. The output depends on the resolved type.
interview.followUp: How can a tag's tree be selected? Append `^{tree}` to the tag name, such as `v1.0.0^{tree}`.

interview.question: How can the displayed commit changes be controlled?
interview.answer: For a commit, git show normally includes its message and textual diff. Options applicable to git diff-tree control how the commit's changes are rendered.
interview.followUp: How does a merge commit differ? Git presents it in the special combined format produced by `git diff-tree --cc`.

keyPoints: The command accepts one or more object names and supports blobs, trees, tags, and commits.
Showing a tag includes its annotation message and the objects it references.
A tree object is displayed as names, matching the effect of `git ls-tree --name-only`.
A blob is emitted as its raw contents rather than as a commit-style diff.
An object expression can select a file's historical contents, for example `next~10:Documentation/README`.
Combining `-s` with `--format=%s` limits output to the selected commit's subject.
gotchas: A commit view includes both the commit message and a textual diff unless options change the output.
Many diff-display controls come from git diff-tree, so output options can substantially change the shown patch.
Merge commits use a combined-diff presentation rather than an ordinary single-parent patch.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git cherry-pick.summary: Apply changes from one or more existing commits to the current branch, recording each as a new commit. The working tree must be clean before the operation.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git cherry-pick.explanation: Git takes the changes introduced by each specified existing commit and applies them to the current branch, creating a separate new commit for each. The working tree must be clean before starting. If a conflict interrupts the operation, resolve the files, stage the resolutions, and continue; or skip the commit, abort the operation, or quit while keeping the current state.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling editing, commit creation, merge-parent selection, signing, and conflict recovery.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: One or more existing commits or revision expressions whose changes should be applied.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git cherry-pick.returns: On success, new commit(s) containing the selected changes are recorded on the current branch; conflict recovery may leave the operation in progress.

example.title: Apply one commit
example.code:
git switch release
git cherry-pick abc1234
example.explanation: Checks out the target branch and applies the selected commit as a new commit.

useCases.title: Backport a targeted fix
useCases.scenario: A fix exists on another branch and must also appear on the release branch.

useCases.title: Transfer specific changes
useCases.scenario: Only selected commits from a larger development line are needed.

useCases.title: Apply a revision range
useCases.scenario: A set of commits is reachable from a source branch but absent from the current branch.

interview.question: What does `git cherry-pick` do?
interview.answer: It applies the changes from existing commits to the current branch and records new commits for them. The source commits themselves are not moved.
interview.followUp: How do you apply only commits reachable from one branch but not the current branch? Use a revision range such as `git cherry-pick ^HEAD master`, which selects those commits and creates new commits on the current branch.

interview.question: How can you apply a commit's changes without committing them immediately?
interview.answer: Use `--no-commit` (`-n`) to apply the changes without making commits. This lets you inspect or combine the resulting changes before creating a commit yourself.
interview.followUp: What prerequisite still applies? The command requires the working tree to be clean before applying the changes.

interview.question: How do you recover from a cherry-pick conflict?
interview.answer: After a conflict, resolve the files and stage the resolutions, then run `git cherry-pick --continue`. You can use `--skip` to omit the problematic commit, `--abort` to return to the pre-operation state, or `--quit` to stop while leaving the current state.
interview.followUp: What happens with a merge commit? Specify the mainline parent with `-m <parent-number>` so Git knows which parent to treat as the baseline.

keyPoints: You can name one commit or several; Git creates a corresponding new commit for each applied change.
Clean or stash local modifications before cherry-picking.
Revision expressions can select a set of commits, such as commits present on `master` but absent from `HEAD`.
gotchas: Start with a clean working tree; uncommitted changes can prevent the operation.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase.summary: Rebase moves selected commits onto a new base by replaying them in order. It can also edit, reorder, omit, or test commits during the replay.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase.explanation: Git rebase selects commits from a branch that are not in the chosen upstream, temporarily rewinds the branch, and reapplies those commits one at a time on a new base. The resulting commits have new identities; conflicts pause the operation for resolution, after which the rebase can continue, skip a commit, or be aborted.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase.syntax:
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>] [<upstream> [<branch>]]
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>] --root [<branch>]
git rebase --continue | --skip | --abort | --quit | --edit-todo | --show-current-patch

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The reference whose excluded commits are selected for replay; if omitted, configured upstream information may be used.

parameters.name: <newbase>
parameters.description: The commit or branch at which the recreated commits begin; defaults to upstream when --onto is absent.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The branch to rebase; if omitted, Git rebases the current branch.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase.returns: The command updates the branch to the rebased history and returns a nonzero status when an operation cannot complete, such as a conflict or failed exec command.

example.title: Rebase a feature branch
example.code:
git switch feature
git rebase main
example.explanation: Moves the commits unique to feature onto the current tip of main. If conflicts occur, resolve them, stage the files, and run git rebase --continue.

useCases.title: Update a feature branch
useCases.scenario: A feature branch started from an older main commit and should incorporate newer main work without a merge commit.

useCases.title: Polish local history interactively
useCases.scenario: A local series of commits needs cleanup before publication.

useCases.title: Validate every recreated commit
useCases.scenario: Each replayed commit should pass a test or lint command.

useCases.title: Transplant a commit range
useCases.scenario: Only commits in a selected range should be moved to a different base.

interview.question: What does git rebase do?
interview.answer: Rebase replays commits from the current branch on top of another base, producing a linear-looking history. Unlike merge, it rewrites the replayed commits rather than creating a merge commit.
interview.followUp: How can a rebase be limited to a different starting point? Use --onto <newbase> with an upstream and optionally a branch.

interview.question: What is the purpose of --onto?
interview.answer: With git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>], Git uses <newbase> as the place where recreated commits begin. The commits selected are those reachable from the branch but excluded by upstream.
interview.followUp: What changes when --root is used? It rebases all commits reachable from the selected branch instead of requiring an upstream boundary.

interview.question: What does interactive rebase allow?
interview.answer: Interactive rebase opens a todo list for the commits being replayed. You can edit that list to reorder commits, combine or edit them, and remove unwanted patches.
interview.followUp: How are conflicts handled? Resolve the conflict, stage the result, then use --continue; --skip omits the problematic commit and --abort restores the pre-rebase state.

keyPoints: Rebase recreates a branch’s selected commits so they sit above a different base commit.
The --onto argument identifies the new base from which the replayed commits are created.
Interactive mode presents the commits in a todo list before replaying them, allowing history editing.
The --exec option runs a shell command after each commit is created during the rebase.
The --root option includes the branch’s complete reachable history rather than selecting commits after an upstream boundary.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase --onto.summary: Use `git rebase --onto` to replay a precise commit range on a different base. Specify the new base, the old boundary, and optionally the branch whose commits should move.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase --onto.explanation: Git first selects commits in <upstream>..<branch>, then replays them onto <newbase>. In `git rebase --onto master next topic`, commits after `next` through `topic` are copied onto `master`; if <branch> is omitted, the current branch is used.

parameters.name: <newbase>
parameters.description: The new starting point for recreated commits; any valid commit is allowed.

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The old boundary; commits reachable from the branch but not this commit are selected.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The branch whose history is rewritten; defaults to HEAD when omitted.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase --onto.returns: Rewrites the selected branch by replaying its selected commits on the new base; the documentation does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Move a selected commit range
example.code:
git switch topic

git rebase --onto master next topic
example.explanation: Replays the commits reachable from topic but not from next onto master. The topic branch is updated to point to the resulting commits.

useCases.title: Transplant a suffix of a topic branch
useCases.scenario: A topic branch includes commits based on an unwanted intermediate branch; transplant only its later commits onto the intended base.

useCases.title: Move a precise commit range
useCases.scenario: A branch contains separate work phases and only the commits after a known boundary belong on another line.

useCases.title: Rebase onto an arbitrary commit
useCases.scenario: The desired starting point is a tag, commit ID, or merge-base expression rather than a branch name.

interview.question: What commit range does `git rebase --onto master next topic` move?
interview.answer: `--onto` specifies the new starting point for the commits being replayed. In `git rebase --onto master next topic`, Git takes commits in `next..topic` and recreates them on `master`.
interview.followUp: How can the current branch be used without naming it? Omit `<branch>`; it defaults to HEAD, provided the other endpoint is present.

interview.question: Explain the operands of the `--onto` form.
interview.answer: The command form is `git rebase --onto <newbase> [<upstream> [<branch>]]`. `<newbase>` is where recreated commits begin, `<upstream>` identifies the old boundary, and `<branch>` names the branch to rewrite.
interview.followUp: Can `<newbase>` be a detached commit? Yes. The documentation says it may be any valid commit, not only an existing branch name.

interview.question: When would you use `--onto` instead of an ordinary rebase?
interview.answer: `--onto` is useful when the branch contains commits based on an unwanted or temporary line. By naming both the old boundary and the branch tip, it selects only the desired suffix and places that suffix on another base.
interview.followUp: What happens if `--onto` is omitted? The upstream commit becomes the starting point for the new commits.

keyPoints: `--onto <newbase>` chooses the commit where Git begins recreating the selected commits.
The new base can be a tag, commit ID, remote-tracking reference, or another valid commit expression.
This three-reference form moves the portion after `next` from `topic` onto `master`.
A second documented pattern moves commits after `topicA` through `topicB` onto `master`.
Before the branch is reset for the operation, Git records its former tip in `ORIG_HEAD`.
A single merge base can be selected with the `A...B` shortcut as a base expression.
gotchas: Rebase moves the selected branch pointer by resetting it to the chosen base before replaying commits, so it rewrites history.
Only one of the range endpoints may be omitted; an omitted endpoint is inferred as HEAD.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase -i.summary: Interactive rebase lets you revise a sequence of commits before sharing it. Edit the generated todo list to reorder, rename, combine, split, or remove commits, then Git reapplies the resulting sequence.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase -i.explanation: Interactive rebase selects commits for rewriting, presents a todo list, and applies the edited instructions in sequence. The list can change commit order, alter messages, combine commits, remove commits, or pause for manual edits; it can also be used to split a commit.

parameters.name: [<upstream> [<branch>]]
parameters.description: Optionally selects the commits' upstream boundary and, when supplied, the branch to rebase.

parameters.name: <newbase>
parameters.description: The new base onto which selected commits are replayed.

parameters.name: -i | --interactive
parameters.description: Runs the rebase interactively and exposes the editable commit todo list.

parameters.name: --exec <cmd>
parameters.description: Runs a command after each rebased commit.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rebase -i.returns: On success, the branch points to the rewritten sequence of commits; if a stop or conflict requires attention, the rebase pauses for the user to resolve or continue.

example.title: Reword the latest local commit
example.code:
git switch -c cleanup
printf 'one\ntwo\n' > notes.txt
git add notes.txt && git commit -m "add notes"
printf 'three\n' >> notes.txt
git add notes.txt && git commit -m "append notes"
git rebase -i HEAD~2
# In the editor, change the second line's command to:
# reword <commit> append notes
# Save, then edit the commit message when prompted.
example.explanation: This creates two local commits and opens an interactive rebase for them. The todo list can be edited to change an operation such as reword; save it and Git pauses when that operation requires input.

useCases.title: Prepare reviewable history
useCases.scenario: Clean up a local feature branch before opening a pull request.

useCases.title: Correct an earlier commit
useCases.scenario: Change a commit message or amend the contents of an earlier commit.

useCases.title: Combine incremental work
useCases.scenario: Fold fix-up commits into the intended preceding change.

useCases.title: Split a commit
useCases.scenario: Separate unrelated changes that were accidentally committed together.

interview.question: What does git rebase -i do?
interview.answer: It opens a todo list for the commits selected by the rebase range, then performs the operations in that list. The list can be edited before Git rewrites the commits.
interview.followUp: How would you split one commit? Start an interactive rebase with the commit to split selected, mark it for editing, then reset, stage subsets, and create replacement commits before continuing.

interview.question: How do you reorder or combine commits?
interview.answer: The todo list is ordered from older commits to newer commits. Reordering lines changes the order in which Git reapplies those commits, while removing a line omits that commit from the rewritten history.
interview.followUp: How can several commits be combined? Mark the later commits with fixup or squash so Git folds them into the preceding commit, with squash allowing message editing.

interview.question: How do you edit a commit during an interactive rebase?
interview.answer: An interactive rebase can stop at a commit marked for editing. After changing files and creating the amended commit, run git rebase --continue to proceed.
interview.followUp: What if a conflict occurs? Resolve the files, stage the resolutions, and run git rebase --continue; use --skip to omit the current commit or --abort to return to the pre-rebase state.

keyPoints: The command first prepares a todo list containing the commits in the selected range.
You can modify the todo list before Git applies the requested history transformation.
Interactive mode supports breaking one existing commit into multiple commits.
Changing line order rearranges commits, while deleting a line excludes that commit from the rewritten result.
Use the commit immediately after the history you want to preserve as the interactive rebase boundary.
The basic form supplies the boundary commit after which Git should open the interactive todo list.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git rerere.sourceTitle: git-rerere - Reuse recorded resolution of conflicted merges
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rerere.summary: git rerere records how you resolve a merge conflict and reapplies that resolution when the corresponding conflict recurs. It is especially useful for repeated rebases and cherry-picks.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rerere.explanation: When enabled, rerere records the conflicted automatic merge state and the manually resolved result. For a later matching conflict, it applies the saved resolution; use status, diff, remaining, forget, clear, or gc to inspect and manage its records.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rerere.syntax: git rerere [clear | forget <pathspec>… | diff | status | remaining | gc]
Rebase & cherry-pick::git rerere.returns: The command reports or updates rerere metadata and conflict-resolution state; its subcommands display status, differences, remaining conflicts, or prune/reset records.

example.title: Record and inspect a rebase conflict resolution
example.code:
git config rerere.enabled true
git rebase main
# Resolve conflicts, then:
git add path/to/file
git rebase --continue
# Inspect or discard a recorded resolution:
git rerere diff
git rerere forget -- path/to/file
example.explanation: Enable rerere before a rebase, resolve a conflict, stage the result, and continue. Git can reuse that recorded resolution when the same conflict recurs.

useCases.title: Repeated rebases
useCases.scenario: A long-lived branch repeatedly rebases onto an evolving main branch and encounters the same conflicts.

useCases.title: Repeated cherry-picks
useCases.scenario: A series of cherry-picks repeatedly produces equivalent conflicts that need the same edits.

useCases.title: Conflict-resolution review
useCases.scenario: A team wants to inspect unresolved paths or compare the current fix with the recorded state.

interview.question: How does git rerere help during repeated rebases?
interview.answer: Enable rerere.enabled, then Git records the automatic conflict result and your hand-resolved result. When the corresponding conflict appears again, Git applies the recorded resolution.
interview.followUp: How can you verify what rerere handled? Use git rerere status for paths whose resolutions will be recorded and git rerere remaining for conflicts it did not autoresolve.

interview.question: Which commands inspect or correct a recorded resolution?
interview.answer: git rerere diff displays the difference between the conflict state and the current resolution. git rerere forget <pathspec> removes the recorded resolution for matching paths in the current conflict.
interview.followUp: What if a resolution is no longer appropriate? Forget it for the affected path, then resolve the conflict manually and let rerere record the corrected result.

interview.question: How does rerere clean up conflict metadata?
interview.answer: git rerere clear resets rerere metadata, which is useful when abandoning a merge. git am --skip/--abort and git rebase --skip/--abort invoke this cleanup automatically.
interview.followUp: How are old records managed? git rerere gc prunes stale records, using gc.rerereUnresolved and gc.rerereResolved to control the default ages.

keyPoints: rerere stores both the automatically produced conflict and your manual resolution.
A later matching automatic conflict can receive the previously saved manual fix.
After configuration, Git normally runs rerere automatically rather than requiring a separate command.
git rerere status shows which conflicted paths are candidates for recording.
git rerere remaining identifies conflicts still needing manual attention.
Committing a merge result also invokes rerere, so an explicit rerere command is not always needed.
gotchas: rerere does nothing until rerere.enabled is configured.
Some conflicts, including conflicting submodules, cannot be autoresolved or tracked.
Automatic garbage collection eventually removes old unresolved and resolved conflict records.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git revert.summary: Undo one or more existing commits by applying their inverse changes and, by default, recording new commits. The original history remains intact, making revert appropriate for shared branches.
Rebase & cherry-pick::git revert.explanation: git revert computes the inverse of one or more existing commits and records that inverse as new commit(s). It normally requires a clean working tree; use --no-commit to apply the inverse only to the index and working tree, or use the continuation commands when resolving a conflict.

parameters.name: --[no-]edit
parameters.description: Suppress the automatic commit message editor or explicitly enable it.

parameters.name: -n, --no-commit
parameters.description: Apply inverse changes without creating commits.

parameters.name: -m <parent-number>, --mainline <parent-number>
parameters.description: Choose the parent line when reverting a merge commit.

parameters.name: -s, --signoff
parameters.description: Add a sign-off trailer to the commit message.

parameters.name: -S[<keyid>], --gpg-sign[=<keyid>]
parameters.description: Sign the commit with the specified key, or the committer's default key.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: Commit or range of commits whose changes should be reversed.

parameters.name: --continue | --skip | --abort | --quit
parameters.description: Resume, omit, cancel, or leave an in-progress revert sequence.

Rebase & cherry-pick::git revert.returns: Creates new commit(s) containing inverse changes, unless -n is used; with -n, only the working tree and index are modified.

example.title: Revert the latest commit
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
git config user.email dev@example.com
git config user.name Dev
echo first > app.txt
git add app.txt && git commit -m "Add app"
echo second >> app.txt
git add app.txt && git commit -m "Extend app"
git revert HEAD --no-edit
git log --oneline -3
example.explanation: Creates two commits, then adds a new commit that reverses the latest one.

useCases.title: Safely undo shared changes
useCases.scenario: A bad commit has already been pushed to a shared branch and should be counteracted without rewriting history.

useCases.title: Prepare changes without committing
useCases.scenario: Several inverse changes need review or combination before one final commit.

useCases.title: Revert a merge
useCases.scenario: A merge introduced unwanted changes and the intended mainline parent is known.

interview.question: How does git revert differ from deleting a commit?
interview.answer: git revert preserves existing history by applying the opposite patch in a new commit. Unlike resetting a branch reference, it is suitable when the original commit is already shared.
interview.followUp: What happens when reverting a merge commit? Use -m <parent-number> to choose the parent whose mainline should be retained, because a merge has multiple parent lines.

interview.question: How can you combine a revert with other changes?
interview.answer: With -n or --no-commit, Git applies the inverse changes to the working tree and index without creating a commit. This allows several reverts to be reviewed or combined before committing.
interview.followUp: Can multiple commits be reverted together? Yes: provide multiple commit arguments or a revision range, then inspect the resulting index and working tree before committing.

interview.question: How do you recover from conflicts during a revert sequence?
interview.answer: A clean working tree is required before starting. If conflicts occur, resolve and stage them, then continue; --skip omits the current commit, --abort restores the pre-revert state, and --quit stops while leaving the current state.
interview.followUp: When would --abort be preferable to --quit? Use --abort to undo the in-progress revert, whereas --quit stops the sequencer without resetting the working tree or index.

keyPoints: The command accepts one or more existing commits and applies the inverse of each commit's introduced changes.
By default, the inverse changes become new commit objects, so the original commits remain in history.
With -n, Git changes only the working tree and index instead of immediately creating a commit.
HEAD~3 identifies the fourth-most-recent commit when used as the target in the documented example.
gotchas: Commit or stash local changes before reverting; the command expects a clean working tree.

Rebase & cherry-pick::Rebase vs merge.summary: Merge preserves the branch join, while rebase replays commits onto another branch to create a linear history. Rebase private work; merge shared work when preserving public ancestry matters.
Rebase & cherry-pick::Rebase vs merge.explanation: Merge combines histories and preserves the point where branches joined. Rebase instead replays the working branch’s commits on top of another branch, producing a linear result; because replayed commits are recreated, use it only when those commits are not already shared with others.
Rebase & cherry-pick::Rebase vs merge.returns: The page documents the rebase operation and its continuation, skipping, and abort controls; it does not define a conventional return value.

example.title: Update a private feature branch
example.code:
git switch feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolve conflicts, then:
git add <file>
git rebase --continue
example.explanation: Rebases a local feature branch onto the updated main branch; use merge instead when the branch history is already shared.

useCases.title: Keep private work linear
useCases.scenario: A local feature branch needs the latest main branch without adding a merge commit.

useCases.title: Preserve shared history
useCases.scenario: A branch has been published or is used by others and its ancestry should remain stable.

useCases.title: Retain merge topology
useCases.scenario: A rebased series contains meaningful internal branch structure that should not be flattened.

interview.question: How do merge and rebase differ?
interview.answer: Merge joins two lines of development and retains their existing ancestry. Rebase replays the working branch’s commits on top of the upstream branch, giving a linear history.
interview.followUp: What should happen if a rebase conflicts? Resolve the conflict, stage the result, and run git rebase --continue; git rebase --abort can abandon the operation.

interview.question: How do you choose between them?
interview.answer: Use rebase for commits that remain private when a linear history is useful. Prefer merge when the commits are already shared, because replaying them changes the history others may rely on.
interview.followUp: Why does replaying matter? Recreated commits can have different identities even when they represent the same changes.

interview.question: What happens to merge commits during rebase?
interview.answer: A standard rebase drops merge commits from its todo list, flattening the rebased portion. Use --rebase-merges when preserving the branching structure is required.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off? Preserving merges retains topology but produces a more complex history than a single linear branch.

keyPoints: Rebase moves a branch’s changes conceptually by replaying its commits above the chosen upstream branch.
Default rebase creates a linearized branch and does not retain merge commits.
Use --rebase-merges when the internal branch topology of the commits being rebased matters.
Conflict handling is iterative: resolve the current commit’s conflict, stage the files, and continue the rebase.
gotchas: Rebase replays commits rather than moving the original commit objects, so commit identities and history can change.
Ordinary rebase omits merge commits unless the rebase-merges option is selected.
After a conflict, resolve the files, stage the resolutions, and continue; skip a problematic commit only when its change is unnecessary.

Rebase & cherry-pick::What cherry-pick i.summary: Git cherry-pick applies the changes introduced by selected existing commits to the current branch. It records a new commit for each selected change, without bringing along the source branch's other commits.
Rebase & cherry-pick::What cherry-pick i.explanation: Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by one or more existing commits to the current branch and records a new commit for each. The working tree must be clean; if a change conflicts, resolve it and continue, or abort the operation.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling editing, committing, merge-parent selection, signing, fast-forwarding, and operation control.

parameters.name: <commit>…
parameters.description: One or more existing commits whose introduced changes should be applied.

Rebase & cherry-pick::What cherry-pick i.returns: Applies each selected commit's change to the current branch and records a new commit for each; conflict-control modes continue, skip, abort, or quit an in-progress operation.

example.title: Copy one commit to another branch
example.code:
git switch release
git cherry-pick <commit>
example.explanation: Switch to the destination branch, then apply the selected commit; Git creates a new commit containing that change.

useCases.title: Backport a fix
useCases.scenario: Bring one bug fix from another branch into a release branch without merging the branch's unrelated work.

useCases.title: Selectively transfer work
useCases.scenario: Apply a small, targeted change from a development branch to the current branch.

useCases.title: Copy a commit range
useCases.scenario: Reapply a range of commits that exist on another line of development but not on the current branch.

keyPoints: Cherry-pick copies the changes introduced by selected existing commits onto the current branch and records separate new commits.
The source can be a branch name, because Git resolves it to the commit at that branch's tip.
Cherry-pick operates on the current branch; it does not switch branches for you.
Revision ranges can select multiple commits, producing new commits for the selected changes.
gotchas: Start with a clean working tree; uncommitted changes can prevent cherry-pick from starting.
After a conflict, the branch does not advance until the cherry-pick is successfully completed.

Rebase & cherry-pick::What rebase is.summary: Rebase reapplies commits from one branch on top of another base tip. It recreates the branch’s commits, producing a rewritten, typically linear history.
Rebase & cherry-pick::What rebase is.explanation: Git identifies the commits on the current branch that are not in the upstream branch, then reapplies those changes starting from the upstream tip. The resulting commits have new identities, producing a linear history; conflicts can pause the operation until you resolve them and continue, skip a commit, or abort the rebase.
Rebase & cherry-pick::What rebase is.syntax:
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [options] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>] [<upstream> [<branch>]]
git rebase [-i | --interactive] [options] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>] --root [<branch>]
git rebase --continue | --skip | --abort | --quit | --edit-todo

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The upstream commit or branch used as the default boundary for selecting commits and, without --onto, as the new starting point.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: The branch whose commits are rebased; if omitted, Git uses the current branch.

parameters.name: <newbase>
parameters.description: The explicit starting point at which Git creates the new commits.

parameters.name: [<upstream> [<branch>]]
parameters.description: The branch or commit range supplied to the rebase operation.

Rebase & cherry-pick::What rebase is.returns: The command updates the branch by creating replacement commits on the selected base; during conflicts it can instead stop for resolution or be continued, skipped, or aborted.

example.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main
example.code:
git switch feature
git rebase main
# Resolve conflicts if Git stops:
git add path/to/resolved-file
git rebase --continue
example.explanation: This reapplies the feature branch's commits after the current tip of main. If a conflict interrupts the operation, resolve the file, stage it, and continue.

useCases.title: Update a feature branch
useCases.scenario: A feature branch is behind the target branch.

useCases.title: Clean up local history
useCases.scenario: Several local commits need a coherent review sequence.

useCases.title: Move commits to another base
useCases.scenario: A branch was created from the wrong starting point.

interview.question: What does rebase do?
interview.answer: Rebase reapplies commits on top of another base tip. It selects the commits reachable from the current branch but not from the upstream, then recreates them beginning at the new base.
interview.followUp: What changes about commit identity? Recreated commits receive new identities because their parent commits change, even when their patch content is equivalent.

interview.question: How do upstream and --onto affect a rebase?
interview.answer: With the usual form, the upstream identifies the boundary and the current branch supplies the commits to replay. The --onto option lets you choose the starting point for the recreated commits explicitly.
interview.followUp: How can a different subset be moved? Use --onto with an upstream boundary and branch, so commits after that boundary are replayed onto the selected new base.

interview.question: What is interactive rebase useful for?
interview.answer: Interactive rebasing lets you edit the list before replaying commits. You can reorder commits and modify the actions assigned to them, which supports cleanup of local history.
interview.followUp: How are conflicts handled? Resolve each conflict, stage the resolution, and run --continue; --skip omits the current commit, while --abort returns to the pre-rebase state.

keyPoints: Rebase replays a branch’s commits above a different base tip, making the branch appear to have begun from that base.
Supplying a branch makes Git switch to it before starting; without one, rebase operates on the current branch.
The new base is the starting point where Git creates the replacement commits.
Interactive mode lets you edit the commits selected for replay before Git applies them.
Interactive mode supports changing commit order, allowing a local history to be reorganized before it is rewritten.
Standard rebase produces a linear branch and drops merge commits from its todo list.
gotchas: Ordinary rebasing omits merge commits from its todo list; use the merge-preserving option when retaining the branch structure matters.
Without an explicit upstream, a detached HEAD or an unconfigured upstream causes the operation to stop.

Remotes & collaboration::Forks and pull.summary: Contribute without push access by forking a project, creating and pushing a topic branch to your copy, and opening a pull request against the original repository. The owner reviews the proposal and may request more commits before merging or closing it.
Remotes & collaboration::Forks and pull.explanation: A fork is a hosting-service copy of a repository in your account when you lack push access to the original. Develop on a topic branch, push that branch to your fork, then open a pull request proposing those commits to the original project; discussion may lead to further commits before the owner merges or closes it.

example.title: Contribute through a fork
example.code:
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/PROJECT.git
cd PROJECT
git switch -c improve-docs
# edit files, then stage and commit
git add .
git commit -m "Improve documentation"
git remote add fork https://github.com/YOU/PROJECT.git
git push -u fork improve-docs
# Open a pull request from improve-docs on the hosting service
example.explanation: The branch is pushed to your fork; create the pull request there so the original project owner can review and merge or close it.

useCases.title: External open-source contribution
useCases.scenario: You want to fix a bug in an open-source project but are not an approved contributor.

useCases.title: Collaborative code review
useCases.scenario: You need review before changes enter a shared repository.

useCases.title: Isolated proposals
useCases.scenario: Several independent changes must be proposed without mixing their histories.

interview.question: How do you contribute when you cannot push to the original repository?
interview.answer: Fork the project, create a topic branch, commit the change, push the branch to your fork, and open a pull request against the original repository. The project owner can discuss the proposal and then merge or close it.
interview.followUp: How can you continue responding to review? Push additional commits to the same branch used by the pull request; the proposal can then be updated before the owner decides.

interview.question: What are the roles of a fork and a pull request?
interview.answer: The fork is a copy under your namespace, where you have permission to push. The pull request connects a branch in that copy with the original project for review and a possible merge.
interview.followUp: What should happen after the original project advances? Synchronize the updated mainline branch back to your fork before starting or refreshing later work.

interview.question: What workflow does the documentation recommend for a contribution?
interview.answer: Use a separate topic branch for the proposed change, make focused commits, push that branch to the fork, and open the pull request from it. This keeps the proposal isolated and makes review clearer.
interview.followUp: Why avoid committing directly on the fork's default branch? An isolated topic branch lets you develop multiple proposals independently and update one review without mixing unrelated work.

keyPoints: Fork the project when the original repository does not grant you push access.
Your fork is an independently writable copy in your hosting-service namespace.
A pull request proposes sending changes from your fork back to the original repository.
Develop the contribution on a topic branch rather than directly on the default branch.
Record the proposed improvement in commits on that topic branch.
Publish the topic branch by pushing it to your fork.
Review discussion can result in additional commits before the proposal is finalized.
The original project owner makes the final decision by merging or closing the pull request.

Remotes & collaboration::git fetch.summary: Downloads refs and the objects needed for their histories from another repository, updating remote-tracking branches without merging into the current branch. Fetched ref names and object IDs are recorded in .git/FETCH_HEAD.
Remotes & collaboration::git fetch.explanation: Git contacts the specified repository, obtains the objects needed for the selected branches or tags, and updates matching remote-tracking references. It also records the fetched reference names and object IDs in .git/FETCH_HEAD; it does not merge those changes into the currently checked-out branch.
Remotes & collaboration::git fetch.syntax:
git fetch [<options>] [<repository> [<refspec>…]]
git fetch [<options>] <group>
git fetch --multiple [<options>] [(<repository> | <group>)…]
git fetch --all [<options>]

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling fetching, pruning, tags, shallow history, ref updates, and output.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: A configured remote name or repository URL.

parameters.name: <refspec>…
parameters.description: A mapping that specifies which remote refs to fetch and which local refs to update.

parameters.name: <group>
parameters.description: A configured group of repositories.

Remotes & collaboration::git fetch.returns: Updates selected local remote-tracking refs and writes fetched ref names and object IDs to .git/FETCH_HEAD; it does not integrate the changes into the current branch.

example.title: Inspect remote changes
example.code:
git fetch origin main

git log --oneline main..origin/main
example.explanation: Fetches the remote main branch, then lists commits present on the remote-tracking branch but not in the local main branch.

useCases.title: Inspect remote updates
useCases.scenario: Review incoming work without changing the checked-out branch.

useCases.title: Fetch all remotes
useCases.scenario: Synchronize several configured remotes in one operation.

useCases.title: Prune stale references
useCases.scenario: Remove local remote-tracking refs deleted from the server.

useCases.title: Control history depth
useCases.scenario: Limit transferred history for a shallow repository.

interview.question: What does git fetch change locally?
interview.answer: It downloads refs and the objects required to complete their histories, then updates remote-tracking branches. It does not merge the fetched branch into the current branch; FETCH_HEAD records the fetched refs and object names.
interview.followUp: How would you fetch only selected history? Use a refspec to select refs, or a shallow option such as --depth=<depth> to limit commits from each remote branch tip.

interview.question: How do you control what git fetch retrieves?
interview.answer: The command accepts a repository and optional refspecs, so it can fetch from one named remote or URL and restrict which refs are obtained. With --all it fetches all configured remotes.
interview.followUp: How can stale remote-tracking refs be removed? Use --prune, which removes remote-tracking references that no longer exist on the remote.

interview.question: What are remote-tracking branches and FETCH_HEAD used for?
interview.answer: Remote-tracking references are updated after the remote refs and necessary objects are received. The fetched ref names and object IDs are written to .git/FETCH_HEAD, which other commands can use to identify what was fetched.
interview.followUp: What does --atomic provide? It makes ref updates transactional: either every ref update succeeds or none is applied.

keyPoints: The command retrieves branches and tags, collectively called refs, from one or more repositories.
Git transfers the objects needed to make the fetched histories complete.
Fetching advances the corresponding remote-tracking branches rather than the checked-out local branch.
Git records fetched ref names and their object IDs in .git/FETCH_HEAD.
The atomic option makes reference updates transactional.
gotchas: A shallow repository may reject refs that would require changing its shallow-boundary file unless you explicitly allow that update.
Repeated fetches replace earlier FETCH_HEAD entries unless you use the option that appends them.

Remotes & collaboration::git fetch --pru.summary: git fetch --prune updates a remote and removes local remote-tracking references for branches that no longer exist there. It cleans references such as origin/*, not the remote branch or your corresponding local branch.
Remotes & collaboration::git fetch --pru.explanation: When fetching from a remote, Git first updates the information it can obtain and removes remote-tracking references for branches that the remote no longer advertises. This affects references such as refs/remotes/origin/*, not the corresponding local branches. The option can be enabled routinely with fetch.prune or a per-remote prune setting.

parameters.name: <name>
parameters.description: Remote name or URL to fetch from; the documentation shows <name> and URL forms.

Remotes & collaboration::git fetch --pru.returns: Updates fetched remote-tracking references and removes stale remote-tracking references; the page does not specify a distinct return value.

example.title: Prune stale remote-tracking references
example.code: git fetch origin --prune
example.explanation: Fetch from origin and remove stale remote-tracking references.

useCases.title: Synchronize branch metadata
useCases.scenario: After teammates delete merged branches on the server, clean obsolete origin/* references while fetching.

useCases.title: Keep remote state accurate
useCases.scenario: Avoid stale branch names in branch listings and scripts that inspect remote-tracking refs.

useCases.title: Automate cleanup
useCases.scenario: Apply pruning routinely without adding the flag to every fetch.

interview.question: What does git fetch --prune remove?
interview.answer: It removes remote-tracking references that no longer exist on the remote, and it does so as part of fetching. It does not delete the remote branch itself or automatically delete a developer’s local branch.
interview.followUp: How can this behavior be applied automatically? Configure fetch.prune globally or set remote.<name>.prune for a particular remote.

interview.question: What is the command form for pruning during a fetch?
interview.answer: Use git fetch --prune <name>, replacing <name> with the remote name such as origin. The fetch still contacts the remote and updates normal fetch data while cleaning stale remote-tracking references.
interview.followUp: How would you clean stale references without fetching? Use git remote prune <name>.

interview.question: How does pruning interact with tags?
interview.answer: The --prune option targets remote-tracking references. Local tags have separate behavior: they are pruned when explicitly included by a refspec, while tags obtained only by default auto-following or --tags are excluded.
interview.followUp: What option explicitly enables pruning of local tags? --prune-tags, used together with --prune; it should be used cautiously because it can remove local tags.

keyPoints: Pruning happens before the fetch operation completes and removes remote-tracking references absent from the remote.
If fetching is unnecessary, git remote prune <name> performs pruning alone.
Enable pruning for regular workflows through the global fetch.prune configuration.
A per-remote prune configuration can limit automatic pruning to a selected remote.
gotchas: Ordinarily, --prune does not remove tags that Git obtained through automatic tag following.
Explicitly fetched tags can also be affected by pruning, so use tag refspecs carefully.

Remotes & collaboration::git pull.summary: Fetches changes from a remote repository and integrates them into the current branch. Depending on configuration or flags, integration uses fast-forward, merge, or rebase.
Remotes & collaboration::git pull.explanation: Git pull first fetches from the selected repository, then integrates the fetched branch heads into the currently checked-out branch. Depending on options or configuration, integration uses merge or rebase; a branch that is merely behind can be fast-forwarded.

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling fetching and integration, including rebase or merge behavior.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: The source remote repository, specified by remote name or URL.

parameters.name: <refspec>…
parameters.description: References to fetch and corresponding local references to update.

Remotes & collaboration::git pull.returns: Updates the current branch by fetching from the specified source and integrating the fetched branch heads.

example.title: Update a branch with rebase
example.code:
git switch main
git pull --rebase origin main
example.explanation: Updates the local main branch from origin/main and replays local commits on top of the fetched history.

useCases.title: Fast-forward routine updates
useCases.scenario: Synchronize a checked-out branch that has no conflicting local commits with its remote-tracking counterpart.

useCases.title: Merge remote changes
useCases.scenario: Bring remote work into a local branch while preserving a merge-based history.

useCases.title: Rebase local work
useCases.scenario: Replay local commits on top of newly fetched remote commits.

useCases.title: Selective reference updates
useCases.scenario: Fetch selected branches or mappings rather than relying on the configured default refspec.

interview.question: What does git pull do internally?
interview.answer: git pull combines fetching and integration. It runs git fetch with the supplied parameters, then uses either git rebase or git merge according to command-line flags and configuration.
interview.followUp: What happens when the branch is only behind the remote? By default, Git fast-forwards the current branch to match the remote.

interview.question: What can the repository argument represent?
interview.answer: The repository argument identifies the source of the fetch or pull operation. It may be a remote name, such as origin, or a repository URL.
interview.followUp: What does a refspec control? It specifies which references are fetched and which local references are updated.

interview.question: How do --rebase and --no-rebase change pull?
interview.answer: With --rebase, pull invokes rebase instead of merge to reconcile the fetched history with the current branch. With --no-rebase, it selects merge explicitly.
interview.followUp: How can this policy be made persistent? Set the corresponding pull.rebase configuration option.

keyPoints: The command integrates remote changes into whichever local branch is currently checked out.
A branch that has no competing local commits can normally be advanced by fast-forwarding.
The first phase fetches using the repository and refspec arguments supplied to pull.
The second phase chooses rebase or merge based on flags and configuration.
The optional repository identifies where Git obtains the updates.
An optional refspec narrows the references fetched and maps them to local references.
gotchas: When local and remote histories have diverged, choose an integration strategy explicitly with --rebase or --no-rebase, or configure pull.rebase.
Without a rebase choice, pull performs the default fetch-then-merge workflow; do not assume it always creates a rebase-style history.

Remotes & collaboration::git pull --reba.summary: Fetches updates from the upstream branch, then rebases the current branch on top of them instead of merging. This reapplies local commits after the fetched upstream tip.
Remotes & collaboration::git pull --reba.explanation: When run on a branch with an upstream, Git first fetches the upstream changes, then rebases the current branch so its local commits are replayed on the updated upstream tip. This replaces the usual merge step; conflicts can require manual resolution before the rebase continues.

parameters.name: [options] [<repository> [<refspec>…]]
parameters.description: Remote and branch or other fetch arguments accepted by git pull; the option --rebase selects rebasing after fetch.

Remotes & collaboration::git pull --reba.returns: The page describes updating the current branch through fetch followed by rebase or merge; it specifies no separate return value.

example.title: Update a branch without a merge commit
example.code: git pull --rebase origin main
example.explanation: Fetches the remote branch and reapplies the current branch's local commits on top of it.

useCases.title: Reconcile diverged work with a linear history
useCases.scenario: A local branch and its upstream both contain new commits.

useCases.title: Keep routine updates free of merge commits
useCases.scenario: A project prefers rebasing local work rather than creating pull merge commits.

useCases.title: Rebase while preserving merge structure
useCases.scenario: Local merge commits must remain represented during the operation.

interview.question: What does git pull --rebase do?
interview.answer: Git pull performs a fetch and then reconciles the fetched branch with the current branch. With --rebase, the reconciliation invokes rebase rather than merge, placing local commits after the updated upstream.
interview.followUp: What does --rebase=merges change? It uses rebase --rebase-merges so local merge commits are included in the rebasing operation.

interview.question: How does --rebase differ from the default merge behavior?
interview.answer: The option accepts a true form that rebases the current branch on top of the upstream after fetching. The false form instead merges the upstream branch into the current branch.
interview.followUp: How can this behavior be configured persistently? Git documents pull.rebase, branch.<name>.rebase, and branch.autoSetupRebase for that purpose.

interview.question: When would a team choose pull --rebase?
interview.answer: The command is useful when the current branch and its upstream have diverged and a linear history is preferred. It fetches first, then reapplies the current branch's local work onto the fetched upstream tip.
interview.followUp: What if interactive editing is needed? The interactive value enables interactive rebase mode.

keyPoints: The operation begins by fetching with the supplied pull parameters.
After fetching, Git chooses rebase or merge according to options and configuration.
The true setting places the current branch above the fetched upstream branch.
The false setting uses a merge instead of replaying commits.
The interactive value enables interactive rebase behavior.
gotchas: A divergent branch requires an explicit reconciliation strategy such as --rebase or --no-rebase.
Use --rebase=merges when local merge commits should be retained during the rebase.
The command can use the remote-tracking branch to avoid replaying changes that are not local.

Remotes & collaboration::git push.summary: Sends required commit objects to a remote repository and updates its branches, tags, or other refs. Use a remote plus branch for common pushes, or a refspec for precise source-to-destination mapping.
Remotes & collaboration::git push.explanation: git push transfers missing objects from the local repository and updates one or more references in a remote repository. The remote can be named explicitly, and a refspec selects the local source and remote destination; when omitted, configured push and upstream settings determine the target.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: Remote repository name or URL receiving the update.

parameters.name: <refspec>…
parameters.description: Source-to-destination reference mapping in the form `[+]<src>[:<dst>]`.

Remotes & collaboration::git push.returns: The page describes updates to remote references and transfer of required objects; it does not specify a conventional return value.

example.title: Publish a branch
example.code: git push -u origin main
example.explanation: Publishes the local main branch to origin and records origin/main as its upstream.

useCases.title: Publish a branch
useCases.scenario: Share a newly committed local branch with collaborators.

useCases.title: Synchronize commits
useCases.scenario: Update a remote branch after adding commits locally.

useCases.title: Use a refspec
useCases.scenario: Map a local branch or object to a differently named remote ref.

useCases.title: Push multiple refs
useCases.scenario: Publish tags or all branches when the workflow requires broader synchronization.

interview.question: What does `git push` do?
interview.answer: It updates remote references from local references and sends objects needed to complete those references. The simplest explicit form names a remote and branch, such as `git push origin main`.
interview.followUp: What does a refspec control? It maps a source object or ref to a destination ref, using the form `[+]<src>[:<dst>]`.

interview.question: How does a refspec work?
interview.answer: A refspec uses `[+]<src>[:<dst>]`. The source identifies what local object or ref to push, while the destination identifies the remote ref to update.
interview.followUp: What does `+` change? It requests a forced update, allowing a non-fast-forward replacement that an ordinary push generally rejects.

interview.question: What is the purpose of `git push -u`?
interview.answer: Without an explicit destination, Git uses its configured push behavior and upstream settings to determine where to push. `-u` or `--set-upstream` records tracking information for a successful push.
interview.followUp: Why is recording an upstream useful? Later commands can use the relationship between the local branch and its remote-tracking branch without repeatedly specifying both names.

keyPoints: Git transfers only the object data required by the selected updates when that data is absent remotely.
The basic form specifies the remote name followed by the local branch to publish.
A refspec may omit the destination, rename the remote destination, or target a specific object expression.
gotchas: A normal push rejects a non-fast-forward update, so it will not overwrite remote work that your local branch does not contain.
In a refspec, the destination controls the remote reference; it must name a branch, tag, or other ref rather than an arbitrary expression.

Remotes & collaboration::git push --forc.summary: Force-updates a remote ref only when its current value matches the expected value. This protects against overwriting remote work that appeared after your last known remote state.
Remotes & collaboration::git push --forc.explanation: The option permits a non-fast-forward update, but first checks a remote branch against an expected value. With the bare form, Git uses the corresponding remote-tracking branch; with an explicit ref and expected object, it compares against that supplied value and aborts if the check fails.

parameters.name: <refname>
parameters.description: Optional remote reference to protect; when omitted, all remote references being updated are protected.

parameters.name: <expect>
parameters.description: Expected current object name for the protected remote reference; an empty value requires that the reference not exist.

Remotes & collaboration::git push --forc.returns: On success, the selected remote reference is updated; if its current value does not satisfy the lease expectation, git push fails.

example.title: Safely publish a rebased branch
example.code:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease origin HEAD:main
example.explanation: Fetch the remote state, rebase local work onto it, then update the remote branch only if its value still matches the fetched remote-tracking state.

useCases.title: Publish rewritten commits while detecting intervening remote updates
useCases.scenario: After rebasing a private branch

useCases.title: Use an explicit expectation independent of the local remote-tracking branch
useCases.scenario: Replacing a remote ref with a known prior object

useCases.title: Use an empty expectation to require that the named ref does not exist
useCases.scenario: Creating a remote ref only if absent

interview.question: What safety check does --force-with-lease provide?
interview.answer: It enables a non-fast-forward push only when the remote reference still has the expected value. If the remote value differs, the push fails instead of overwriting newer remote work.
interview.followUp: How does the bare form choose its expectation? It requires each remote reference being updated to equal its local remote-tracking branch.

interview.question: How does the explicit ref-and-expectation form work?
interview.answer: The explicit form names one reference and an expected object: --force-with-lease=<refname>:<expect>. Git compares that expected object with the current remote value; the expectation may differ from the local remote-tracking branch.
interview.followUp: What does an empty <expect> mean? The named remote reference must not already exist.

interview.question: How does this differ from an unconditional force push?
interview.answer: A normal push generally rejects replacing a remote ref unless the new value fast-forwards it. This option overrides that restriction conditionally, retaining a check that the remote is at the value you intended to replace.
interview.followUp: Why can an implicit background fetch be risky? It can change the remote-tracking value used by the bare lease before the push runs.

keyPoints: It allows a non-fast-forward replacement only when the remote reference matches the expected value.
A mismatch makes the push fail, preventing the overwrite.
Without further arguments, the option protects every remote reference that the push would update.
The bare form uses each local remote-tracking branch as its expected remote state.
Supplying only a reference limits protection to that named reference and uses its remote-tracking branch as the expectation.
The fully specified form checks one named reference against the explicitly supplied expected object.
An explicit expectation does not need to equal the locally stored remote-tracking value.
gotchas: The bare form can be undermined when background processes fetch the same remote, because they may update the remote-tracking branch used as the expectation.
An empty expected value means the selected remote reference is required to be absent.

Remotes & collaboration::git remote.summary: Manage named repositories whose branches the local repository tracks. `git remote` can list, add, rename, remove, inspect, and reconfigure remotes, including their fetch and push URLs.
Remotes & collaboration::git remote.explanation: A remote is a named reference to another repository whose branches this repository tracks. The command manages that reference: it can add, rename, remove, inspect, select tracked branches, configure fetch or push URLs, and set the remote-tracking branch’s symbolic HEAD.

git remote rename <old> <new>
git remote remove <name>
git remote set-head <name> (-a | --auto | -d | --delete | <branch>)
git remote set-branches [--add] <name> <branch>…
git remote get-url [--push] [--all] <name>
git remote set-url [--push] <name> <newurl> [<oldurl>]
git remote set-url --add [--push] <name> <newurl>
git remote set-url --delete [--push] <name> <url>
git remote [-v | --verbose] show [-n] <name>…

parameters.description: Remote name, such as `origin`.

parameters.name: <URL>
parameters.description: Repository URL associated with the remote.

parameters.name: <old>

parameters.name: <new>
parameters.description: New remote name when renaming.

parameters.name: <branch>
parameters.description: Branch name used by tracking, HEAD selection, or branch filtering.

parameters.name: <newurl> / <oldurl> / <url>
parameters.description: Replacement, additional, or removable remote URL.

example.code:

git remote -v
git remote get-url origin
example.explanation: Adds a remote named origin, lists its fetch and push URLs, then prints the URL configured for that remote.
