useCases.scenario: A project needs a named upstream repository for fetch and push operations.

useCases.title: Update a remote URL
useCases.scenario: A hosting migration changes the repository endpoint without changing scripts that use the remote name.

useCases.title: Limit tracked branches
useCases.scenario: A repository should track only selected branches from a remote.

useCases.title: Inspect collaboration configuration
useCases.scenario: A team wants to inspect remote URLs, branches, and tracking state.

interview.question: What is a Git remote?
interview.answer: A remote is a named repository reference used for tracking branches and exchanging commits. `git remote` manages its URLs, tracked branches, remote HEAD, and related configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect both configured directions? Use `git remote -v`; it displays the fetch and push URLs for each remote.

interview.question: How do you add a remote?
interview.answer: `git remote add <name> <URL>` creates a remote with the supplied name and URL. It can also configure tracked branches, tags, mirroring, and optionally fetch immediately.
interview.followUp: How can you add a remote without fetching every branch? Use `-t <branch>` to limit the tracked branch configuration.

interview.question: How do you change a remote URL?
interview.answer: `git remote set-url` changes an existing remote URL. Its `--push` form changes the push URL, while `--add` and `--delete` manage multiple URLs.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies when fetch and push URLs differ? They may differ, but they must still identify the same repository.

keyPoints: The command manages named repositories whose branches are tracked by the local repository.
Running `git remote` lists configured remote names; `-v` or `--verbose` adds their URLs.
`add` supports branch selection, an initial fetch, tag control, and fetch or push mirroring.
`rename` changes a remote’s name and updates the related remote-tracking references and configuration.
`set-head` sets, discovers, or deletes the symbolic branch that represents a remote’s default branch.
`set-branches` replaces or extends the branches configured for remote tracking.
gotchas: Separate push and fetch URLs are allowed, but the documentation requires them to refer to the same repository location.

Remotes & collaboration::git submodule.summary: git submodule embeds another Git repository inside a subdirectory of a superproject. The superproject records the submodule commit it uses, while the embedded repository keeps its own history.
Remotes & collaboration::git submodule.explanation: A submodule places another Git repository at a path inside the superproject while retaining that repository's separate history. The superproject records the submodule commit to use; .gitmodules supplies shared path and URL configuration, while local configuration is initialized when needed.

parameters.name: <repository>
parameters.description: Repository URL or local repository used by add.

parameters.name: [<path>]
parameters.description: Filesystem path where the submodule is placed; if omitted, Git derives it from the repository name.

parameters.name: [<path>…​]
parameters.description: One or more submodule paths for status, init, update, deinit, set-branch, set-url, or summary.

Remotes & collaboration::git submodule.returns: The command initializes, updates, inspects, and manages submodules; individual subcommands may modify the working tree or configuration and report status.

example.title: Add and initialize a submodule
example.code:
git submodule add https://github.com/example/lib.git vendor/lib
git submodule update --init --recursive
git add .gitmodules vendor/lib
git commit -m "Add library submodule"
example.explanation: Adds the repository under vendor/lib, checks out the recorded submodule commit, stages the submodule metadata and gitlink, then records the change.

useCases.title: Pin an external dependency
useCases.scenario: A project depends on a separately versioned library and should record exactly which library revision it builds.

useCases.title: Include shared components
useCases.scenario: A repository contains reusable code maintained in another repository but needs it available under a stable directory.

useCases.title: Initialize a fresh checkout
useCases.scenario: A checkout includes submodules whose working directories have not yet been populated.

useCases.title: Inspect dependency state
useCases.scenario: A team needs to verify each embedded repository's checked-out revision.

interview.question: What is a Git submodule?
interview.answer: A submodule is another Git repository stored below a directory in the superproject. The superproject records which submodule commit it uses, while the submodule retains its own history.
interview.followUp: How do you make a fresh checkout usable? Run git submodule update --init, adding --recursive when nested submodules must also be initialized.

interview.question: What does git submodule add do?
interview.answer: git submodule add records the repository and path in the next superproject changeset. It also creates or updates .gitmodules, which provides shared submodule configuration.
interview.followUp: How can local configuration be populated from that file? Use git submodule init, which sets submodule.$name.url in .git/config using .gitmodules as a template.

interview.question: How can you inspect submodule state?
interview.answer: git submodule status reports the currently checked-out commit for each submodule, together with its path and git describe output. This helps inspect whether the working checkout matches the expected state.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when nested modules are involved? Use the recursive status or update forms so descendants are inspected or initialized as well.

keyPoints: It embeds a separate repository beneath a directory in the current repository.
The repository containing the submodule is called the superproject.
Use add with a repository and optional path to register the embedded repository.
Adding a submodule schedules its path and reference for inclusion in the superproject's next commit.
The command group supports inspection, initialization, updating, branch and URL configuration, removal, and summaries.
Initialization copies the effective submodule URL into local Git configuration.
gotchas: Changes inside the submodule belong to its separate history; committing the superproject does not merge those commits into the superproject's history.
A clone or checkout may require initialization before the recorded submodule contents are available.
Use status to verify the checked-out commit rather than assuming the submodule is at the superproject's intended commit.

Remotes & collaboration::Upstream tracki.summary: An upstream tracking branch links a local branch with a remote branch. Git then knows which branch to compare against and which upstream to use for argument-less pull and related operations.
Remotes & collaboration::Upstream tracki.explanation: An upstream tracking branch is a local branch configuration that names a remote and remote branch as its counterpart. Git uses that relationship to report ahead/behind status, choose the source for an argument-less pull, and provide defaults for some remote operations; it can be created during branch creation or assigned later.

parameters.name: <upstream>
parameters.description: The remote-tracking or remote branch to treat as the local branch’s upstream.

parameters.name: <branchname>
parameters.description: The local branch whose tracking configuration is changed; defaults to the current branch.

Remotes & collaboration::Upstream tracki.returns: Updates the selected local branch’s upstream tracking configuration.

example.title: Create and configure a tracking branch
example.code:
git switch -c feature origin/main
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/feature

git status
git pull
git push
example.explanation: Creates a local branch from a remote-tracking branch, explicitly links it to the corresponding remote branch, then uses the relationship for status, pull, and push.

useCases.title: Create a local branch from a remote-tracking branch
useCases.scenario: Start work from a fetched remote branch while retaining its counterpart for comparison and synchronization.

useCases.title: Set or change an upstream
useCases.scenario: Attach an existing local branch to a remote branch after fetching or changing collaboration targets.

useCases.title: Review branch relationship
useCases.scenario: Inspect whether a local branch is ahead of, behind, or related to its upstream.

useCases.title: Pull from the configured upstream
useCases.scenario: Use an argument-less pull that resolves its source from the checked-out branch’s configuration.

interview.question: What is an upstream tracking branch used for?
interview.answer: A tracking branch is a local branch with an upstream relationship to a remote branch. Git can use it to show the relationship in status and branch -v, and argument-less pull uses the configured upstream.
interview.followUp: How can an existing local branch be linked? Use git branch --set-upstream-to=<upstream> [<branchname>]; omitting the local branch selects the current branch.

interview.question: How is tracking configured when creating a branch?
interview.answer: When a new branch starts from a remote-tracking branch, Git normally establishes tracking configuration. The --track option can request this explicitly, while --no-track disables it.
interview.followUp: What does --track=inherit do? It copies the upstream configuration of the start-point branch rather than using the start-point branch itself.

interview.question: How do you change the upstream of an existing branch?
interview.answer: Use git branch --set-upstream-to=<upstream> [<branchname>] to assign an upstream to an existing local branch. The upstream identifies the remote branch Git should treat as that local branch’s counterpart.
interview.followUp: How can the relationship be inspected? git status and git branch -v display the relationship when tracking configuration exists.

keyPoints: Starting a local branch from a remote-tracking branch normally creates its upstream relationship automatically.
The relationship is stored through branch-specific remote and merge configuration entries.
Tracking lets status and branch -v expose how the local and upstream branches relate.
After checkout, git pull with no arguments uses the configured upstream as its source.
The set-upstream operation declares which remote branch is considered the local branch’s upstream.
Direct tracking uses the branch supplied as the creation start point as the new branch’s upstream.
gotchas: Running --set-upstream-to without a branch name changes the current branch, which can accidentally configure the wrong branch if the checkout is unexpected.
Inherited tracking does not necessarily point at the start-point branch itself; it copies that branch’s upstream configuration.
The meaning of tracking depends on the selected mode, so --track, --track=direct, and --track=inherit should not be treated as interchangeable.

Undoing & recovering::git clean.summary: Delete untracked files from the working tree, optionally including directories and ignored files. Preview or interact before destructive cleanup, and use pathspecs or exclusions to control its scope.
Undoing & recovering::git clean.explanation: Run git clean from a repository to recursively remove untracked content beneath the current directory. It normally targets files Git does not know about and leaves ignored files alone; choose a preview, interactive mode, or explicit force before deletion, and use pathspecs or exclusions to narrow the operation.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options controlling force, preview, interaction, quiet output, exclusions, ignored-file handling, and directory removal.

parameters.name: pathspec
parameters.description: Files or directories to which cleaning is limited.

Undoing & recovering::git clean.returns: Removes selected untracked files and, with -d, untracked directories; preview and interactive modes do not perform deletion.

example.title: Preview and remove untracked content
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
mkdir -p demo-clean/dist demo-clean/tmp
printf 'build\n' > demo-clean/dist/output.txt
printf 'scratch\n' > demo-clean/tmp/notes.txt
cd demo-clean
git init -q
git clean -n -d
git clean -f -d
example.explanation: Previews untracked files and directories, then removes them after explicitly supplying force and directory options.

useCases.title: Reset generated workspace files
useCases.scenario: Remove build output and other untracked artifacts before rebuilding.

useCases.title: Preview cleanup safely
useCases.scenario: Inspect prospective deletions before making any changes.

useCases.title: Limit cleanup with a pathspec
useCases.scenario: Clean only selected files or directories under a path.

useCases.title: Clean ignored artifacts with -X
useCases.scenario: Remove ignored build products while retaining manually created untracked files.

interview.question: What does git clean do, and what does a pathspec change?
interview.answer: It removes untracked files recursively from the working tree, beginning at the current directory. By default, ignored files are excluded, and supplied pathspecs limit which matching paths are affected.
interview.followUp: How would you clean generated files while preserving ignored files? Use -X, which removes only files ignored by Git.

interview.question: How can you safely inspect or authorize a cleanup?
interview.answer: Use -n to display what would be removed without deleting anything, or -i to choose interactively. Actual deletion normally needs -f because clean.requireForce protects the working tree.
interview.followUp: How can you remove untracked directories as well? Add -d; a nested repository may additionally require a second -f.

interview.question: What is the difference between -x and -X?
interview.answer: The -x option ignores standard ignore rules, while still honoring exclusions supplied with -e; it can therefore remove ignored build products. The -X option has the narrower inverse purpose: remove only ignored files.
interview.followUp: How would you keep a particular generated pattern while using -x? Supply an appropriate -e exclusion pattern on the command line.

keyPoints: The command recursively removes files outside version control, starting from the current directory.
Without -x, ignored files remain; -x includes them in the cleanup.
Pathspec arguments restrict cleanup to matching paths.
Use -d when untracked directories should be deleted along with files.
The -n option previews the planned cleanup without changing files.
The -i option presents an interactive cleanup mode.
The -e option adds an exclusion pattern while normal ignore rules remain active.
gotchas: Deletion normally requires -f, -n, or -i unless clean.requireForce is configured false.
A nested repository directory is protected by default; removing it requires supplying -f twice.
The -x option can remove ignored files too, so use it cautiously and retain any needed command-line exclusions.

Undoing & recovering::git commit --amend.summary: Replace the current branch's latest commit with a new commit. Use it to revise the message or include additional staged content you forgot.
Undoing & recovering::git commit --amend.explanation: Git rebuilds the current branch tip as a new commit from the staged tree. With no explicit message option, the previous commit message becomes the starting point; use --no-edit to retain it unchanged or provide -m, -F, or -c to choose another message.

parameters.name: --amend
parameters.description: Optionally selects the current branch tip for replacement; normal commit options and pathspecs determine the recorded tree and message.

parameters.name: --no-edit
parameters.description: Suppresses changing the existing commit message when used with amend.

parameters.name: -m <msg>
parameters.description: Supplies a replacement commit message.

Undoing & recovering::git commit --amend.returns: A new commit replacing the tip of the current branch.

example.title: Amend the latest commit
example.code:
git add forgotten-file.txt
git commit --amend --no-edit

# Or replace the message too:
git commit --amend -m "Corrected message"
example.explanation: Stage the omitted change, then replace the current branch tip while retaining or replacing the previous message.

useCases.title: Correct the last message
useCases.scenario: A typo or unclear wording remains in the latest commit message.

useCases.title: Add forgotten staged changes
useCases.scenario: A file or fix was omitted from the latest commit.

useCases.title: Polish an unpublished commit
useCases.scenario: The latest commit needs both content and message corrections before sharing.

interview.question: What does git commit --amend do?
interview.answer: It replaces the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit. Git builds that commit from the index and uses the original message as the starting point when no command-line message option is supplied.
interview.followUp: What does --no-edit change? It keeps the existing message without opening an editor, while the commit still gets rebuilt from the prepared tree.

interview.question: How do you add forgotten content to the last commit?
interview.answer: The staged tree is used to construct the replacement commit. Therefore, stage the forgotten file or fix first, then run the amend command.
interview.followUp: How can you amend only selected paths? Use the command's normal explicit pathspec behavior and ensure the intended index or path selection is prepared.

interview.question: How do you change only the last commit's message?
interview.answer: Use git commit --amend with a message option such as -m, -F, or -c. If no such option is used, the previous message supplies the starting point.
interview.followUp: When should the operation be avoided? Since it replaces the branch tip with a new commit, coordinate carefully if that tip is already relied on by others.

keyPoints: The option replaces the current branch tip with a newly created commit.
The replacement uses Git's normal tree preparation, including relevant index, option, and pathspec effects.
If no message option is supplied, the old commit message is loaded as the starting message.
Amend starts from the previous message rather than presenting an empty commit message.
Interactive or otherwise selected input options can affect the tree recorded by the amended commit.
gotchas: Amending creates a replacement commit rather than editing the existing commit object.
Without a new message option, Git opens the prior message as the starting content; this is not the same as explicitly preserving it with --no-edit.
Only staged content and any explicitly selected paths contribute to the replacement commit, so stage forgotten files first.

Undoing & recovering::git filter-repo.summary: git-filter-repo is the recommended modern replacement for git filter-branch when rewriting substantial repository history. Use it to remove a file or other data from every commit, with coordination because rewritten history changes commit identities.
Undoing & recovering::git filter-repo.explanation: git-filter-repo is a separately distributed history-rewriting tool recommended as a replacement for filter-branch. It can rewrite repository history to remove a selected path from every commit; the rewritten commits have different identities, so collaborators must coordinate before replacing shared history.

example.title: Remove a sensitive file from history
example.code: git filter-repo --path passwords.txt --invert-paths
example.explanation: Removes passwords.txt from the repository’s rewritten history.

useCases.title: Purge sensitive data
useCases.scenario: Remove a committed secret or other sensitive file from every historical commit.

useCases.title: Remove a path
useCases.scenario: Delete an obsolete path from all revisions of a repository.

useCases.title: Rewrite repository history
useCases.scenario: Perform a large, scriptable rewrite that would otherwise use filter-branch.

keyPoints: git-filter-repo is a Python-based replacement for filter-branch.
Use it for broad, scriptable history rewrites that would otherwise require filter-branch.
A primary use is removing a file throughout the repository's history.
History rewriting can affect a large portion of the repository, not merely the current checkout.
Coordinate carefully if others have already built work on the commits being rewritten.
gotchas: The Git documentation points to the tool's external documentation and source rather than documenting its options or complete command syntax on git-scm.com.
Do not choose filter-branch for this task; Git recommends git-filter-repo instead.

Undoing & recovering::git reflog.summary: git reflog manages local reference logs: records of where HEAD, branches, and other references have pointed. Use its entries and selectors such as HEAD@{2} to inspect or recover earlier positions, including commits no longer reachable from current history.
Undoing & recovering::git reflog.explanation: A reflog is a local record of updates to a reference, such as HEAD or a branch. Use the ordinary form to display entries, then address an earlier state with a selector such as HEAD@{2} or a date-based selector; these selectors can identify commits even after they stop being reachable from the current branch history.
Undoing & recovering::git reflog.syntax:
git reflog [show] [<log-options>] [<ref>]
git reflog list
git reflog exists <ref>
git reflog write <ref> <old-oid> <new-oid> <message>
git reflog delete [--rewrite] [--updateref] [--dry-run | -n] [--verbose] <ref>@{<specifier>}…
git reflog drop [--all [--single-worktree] | <refs>…]
git reflog expire [--expire=<time>] [--expire-unreachable=<time>] [--rewrite] [--updateref] [--stale-fix] [--dry-run | -n] [--verbose] [--all [--single-worktree] | <refs>…]

parameters.name: <ref>
parameters.description: Optional reference whose reflog is displayed; defaults to HEAD when omitted.

parameters.name: <log-options>
parameters.description: Revision-log formatting and filtering options accepted by the display form.

parameters.name: <ref>
parameters.description: A reference for which existence is checked, or whose reflog is otherwise operated on.

parameters.name: <specifier>
parameters.description: A reflog selector such as ref@{2} or ref@{one.week.ago}.

Undoing & recovering::git reflog.returns: Displays reflog entries or performs the requested reflog-management operation; the documentation does not define a value-style return.

example.title: Inspect and recover an earlier HEAD position
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
git commit --allow-empty -m initial
git branch feature
git switch feature
git commit --allow-empty -m feature
git switch main
git reflog --date=iso
# Recover a prior HEAD position:
git show HEAD@{1}
example.explanation: Creates several local reference movements, displays HEAD's reflog, and inspects an earlier HEAD position using reflog syntax.

useCases.title: Locate an earlier position for recovery
useCases.scenario: Accidental reset, rebase, or checkout moved a reference.

useCases.title: Find an otherwise unreachable commit
useCases.scenario: A commit is missing from the current branch graph.

useCases.title: Review local reference changes
useCases.scenario: You need to audit recent local branch or HEAD movements.

useCases.title: Manage reflog retention
useCases.scenario: You need to remove or age out reflog records.

interview.question: What does git reflog record, and what does HEAD@{2} mean?
interview.answer: It records local updates to the tips of branches and other references, including HEAD. Entries let Git resolve historical positions such as HEAD@{2}, meaning the value from two reference movements ago.
interview.followUp: How would you recover a commit after a reset? Find its earlier HEAD entry with git reflog, then create or move a branch to that object, for example git branch recovery HEAD@{2}.

interview.question: How do you inspect an earlier branch position?
interview.answer: Run git reflog, optionally supplying a reference such as a branch name. The command shows the reference's recorded movements; reflog selectors can then be used anywhere Git accepts an object name.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect a branch's previous location by date? Use a date-based selector such as master@{one.week.ago}, interpreted in the local repository.

interview.question: Why can reflog recover commits that normal history cannot show?
interview.answer: Reflogs are maintained in the local repository and document local reference updates. They are useful for recovery, but they do not become shared branch history when you fetch or push.
interview.followUp: What limits recovery? Reflog entries can expire, so a commit that is no longer reachable may eventually have no remaining reflog reference.

keyPoints: Reflogs track updates to branch tips and other references in the local repository.
A selector such as HEAD@{2} names HEAD's position two movements earlier.
Reflog selectors can use a time expression to address where a branch pointed at an earlier date.
Besides displaying entries, git reflog provides subcommands for listing, checking, deleting, dropping, writing, and expiring reflog data.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --hard.summary: Move the current branch to a chosen commit and make both the index and working tree match it. With --hard, local tracked changes are discarded, and some untracked files may also be overwritten or deleted.
Undoing & recovering::git reset --hard.explanation: Git first moves the current branch’s HEAD to the selected commit, then makes the index match that commit and the working tree match the index. With --hard, tracked changes after the target commit are discarded; files tracked there but absent from the target are removed, and obstructing untracked files may also be deleted.

parameters.name: --hard
parameters.description: Reset mode; --hard updates both the index and working tree.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: Commit or other revision identifying the state to reset to; defaults to HEAD when omitted.

parameters.name: -q
parameters.description: Suppresses the usual output.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --hard.returns: No documented return value; the command updates the current branch, index, and working tree.

example.title: Discard a local commit and working-tree changes
example.code:
git switch -c reset-demo
echo draft > draft.txt
git add draft.txt
git commit -m "Add draft"
echo discarded >> draft.txt
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git status --short
example.explanation: The final command should show a clean worktree: the branch moves back one commit, the index is reset, and the tracked file changes are discarded.

useCases.title: Remove unwanted local commits
useCases.scenario: Abandon recent local commits that should no longer be part of the branch.

useCases.title: Discard local edits
useCases.scenario: Return the index and working tree to the current commit while keeping the branch pointer unchanged.

useCases.title: Return to a prior state
useCases.scenario: Restore the branch and files to a known earlier revision after a mistaken local change.

interview.question: What does git reset --hard do?
interview.answer: It moves the current branch to the specified commit, resets the index to that commit, and makes the working tree match the index. Local tracked changes after the target are discarded.
interview.followUp: What happens to a tracked file absent from the target commit? It is removed so the working tree matches the target tree.

interview.question: What does git reset --hard with no commit reset to?
interview.answer: With no explicit commit, the command targets HEAD. It therefore leaves the branch pointer where it is while clearing staged and working-tree changes relative to HEAD.
interview.followUp: How does that differ from --soft? --soft moves only the branch pointer and leaves both the index and working tree unchanged.

interview.question: When is --hard suitable for undoing commits?
interview.answer: It is appropriate for abandoning local commits or changes when they should no longer exist locally. The documentation demonstrates moving back three commits with HEAD~3 and warns against doing so after sharing those commits.
interview.followUp: How can a discarded branch position sometimes be located? Git records previous HEAD positions in reflogs, although uncommitted working-tree changes are not thereby restored.

keyPoints: The working tree is rewritten to match the selected commit’s files and directories.
A tracked path present in the current tree but absent from the target is deleted.
After the branch moves, the index is synchronized with the new HEAD, leaving nothing staged.
HEAD~3 is a revision example for moving the branch back three commits.
gotchas: Untracked files can also be overwritten when Git needs to write tracked files from the target commit.
Avoid using this to remove commits that have already been shared, because rewriting the branch history can disrupt collaborators.
Changes to tracked files made after the target commit are thrown away.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --mixed.summary: Moves the current branch’s HEAD to a chosen commit, updates the index to that commit, and leaves the working directory unchanged. As a result, the retained file changes are no longer staged.
Undoing & recovering::git reset --mixed.explanation: With a target commit, Git moves the current branch's HEAD to that commit and makes the index match it. In mixed mode, the working directory is left unchanged, so changes from the moved-back commits remain as unstaged modifications. The target defaults to HEAD, and mixed mode is the default reset mode.

parameters.name: --mixed [-N]
parameters.description: Reset mode; for this card, use `--mixed`, optionally with `-N`.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: Commit at which the current branch HEAD should point; defaults to HEAD.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --mixed.returns: The command updates the branch pointer and index according to the selected target and reports paths that were not updated; it leaves the working directory unchanged in mixed mode.

example.title: Undo the latest commit but keep its changes
example.code:
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
# Edit the files, then inspect and selectively stage them
git status
git add path/to/file
example.explanation: Moves the current branch back one commit while leaving that commit's changes in the working directory, unstaged for review.

useCases.title: Keep changes from an undone commit
useCases.scenario: Undo the latest local commit while preserving its file changes for revision.

useCases.title: Unstage changes
useCases.scenario: Remove all current staged changes without changing the files in the working directory.

useCases.title: Rework local history
useCases.scenario: Move a local branch back to an earlier commit while retaining later work as modifications.

interview.question: What does `git reset --mixed` change?
interview.answer: `git reset --mixed <commit>` moves the current branch’s HEAD to the specified commit and updates the index to that commit’s contents. It deliberately leaves the working directory unchanged, so existing changes are preserved but become unstaged.
interview.followUp: What happens when the commit is omitted? The target defaults to HEAD, so mixed reset can be used to unstage changes without moving the branch.

interview.question: Is `--mixed` required explicitly?
interview.answer: Mixed mode is the default reset mode, so `git reset <commit>` has the same mode behavior when no other mode is supplied. It updates the index while leaving the working directory unchanged.
interview.followUp: How can removed paths be handled differently? Add `-N`; removed paths are marked as intent-to-add.

interview.question: What is the command syntax for mixed reset?
interview.answer: The command accepts a mode and an optional commit in the form `git reset [--soft | --mixed [-N] | --hard | --merge | --keep] [-q] [<commit>]`. For mixed reset, the relevant form is `git reset --mixed [-N] [<commit>]`.
interview.followUp: What does a path-specific reset imply? The official documentation distinguishes the commit-reset form from path-limited forms; a path can limit index changes without moving the branch.

keyPoints: The operation relocates the current branch’s HEAD to the selected commit.
If no target commit is supplied, HEAD is used as the target.
Mixed reset does not rewrite files in the working directory.
The index is synchronized with the new HEAD, removing staged status from the affected changes.
gotchas: The `-N` option changes how removed paths are represented: Git marks them as intent-to-add instead of treating them as ordinary unstaged removals.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --soft.summary: Moves the current branch back to a chosen commit while leaving the index and working-tree files unchanged. Changes remain staged so they can be reviewed, edited, or recommitted.
Undoing & recovering::git reset --soft.explanation: Use the soft mode when you want to move the current branch to an earlier commit without changing either the staging area or working-tree files. Changes introduced by commits after the target remain staged, so you can inspect them, amend them, or create a replacement commit.

parameters.name: --soft
parameters.description: The reset mode; --soft moves HEAD without changing the index or working tree.

parameters.name: <commit>
parameters.description: The commit at which the current branch's HEAD should point.

Undoing & recovering::git reset --soft.returns: No value is returned; the command updates the current branch reference and leaves the index and working tree unchanged in soft mode.

example.title: Combine the latest commit with its parent
example.code:
git switch -c rewrite-demo
printf 'one\n' > note.txt
git add note.txt
git commit -m "Add note"
printf 'two\n' >> note.txt
git add note.txt
git commit -m "Extend note"
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git commit -m "Add complete note"
example.explanation: Creates two commits, moves the current branch back one commit, and recommits the retained changes as one commit.

useCases.title: Squash local commits
useCases.scenario: Several recent commits should become one logical commit.

useCases.title: Redo a commit
useCases.scenario: A commit should be undone while its content remains ready to commit again.

useCases.title: Recover from an operation
useCases.scenario: A merge, rebase, pull, or similar operation needs to be undone without discarding local file changes.

interview.question: What does git reset --soft change?
interview.answer: It moves the current branch's HEAD to the chosen commit while leaving both the index and working tree unchanged. Consequently, changes between the old HEAD and target remain staged for a new commit.
interview.followUp: What happens to unstaged edits already present? They remain untouched too, which can make the resulting staged state harder to interpret.

interview.question: How can --soft be used to combine recent commits?
interview.answer: The target commit is supplied as the optional commit argument, and the command changes which commit HEAD points to. With --soft, Git stops after moving the branch pointer; it does not rewrite the index or files.
interview.followUp: How would you combine several recent commits? Reset to the commit immediately before them, then create one replacement commit from the staged result.

interview.question: When is --soft preferable to --mixed or --hard?
interview.answer: A soft reset is suited to undoing a commit while preserving its content in the staging area. After reviewing or editing that staged content, commit it again with a new message or structure.
interview.followUp: Why might this be confusing when the worktree is dirty? Unstaged edits are preserved alongside the staged commit changes, so status may show multiple sources of changes.

keyPoints: The operation moves the current branch's HEAD to the selected commit.
Soft mode preserves both tracked files in the working tree and the index exactly as they were.
It can help undo commits as well as larger operations such as merges, rebases, and pulls.
A documented workflow resets five commits back and immediately creates a replacement commit.
Resetting to an earlier commit lets several recent commits be consolidated into one.
gotchas: Existing unstaged working-tree edits survive the reset, so distinguish them from the staged changes you intend to recommit.

Undoing & recovering::git restore.summary: Restore selected paths in the working tree, index, or both without creating a commit. Use it to discard working-tree edits, unstage paths, or copy content from another commit.
Undoing & recovering::git restore.explanation: git restore copies selected path content from a restore source into the working tree, the index, or both. Without --staged, the default source is the index; with --staged, the default source is HEAD. Use --source to choose another tree or commit, and provide --worktree with --staged when both locations should change.
Undoing & recovering::git restore.syntax:
git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] <pathspec>…
git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] --pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]
git restore (-p|--patch) [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] [<pathspec>…]

parameters.name: <options>
parameters.description: Options controlling source selection, destination, patch mode, pathspec input, and other behavior.

parameters.name: <tree>
parameters.description: Tree, commit, or other tree object supplying the content when --source is used.

parameters.name: <pathspec>…
parameters.description: One or more paths to restore; -- separates options from paths.

parameters.name: <file>
parameters.description: File containing pathspecs when --pathspec-from-file is selected.

Undoing & recovering::git restore.returns: The command restores the selected paths; it does not create a commit or update the branch.

example.title: Unstage, discard, and restore from another commit
example.code:
git restore --staged app.js
git restore app.js
git restore --source=HEAD~1 --worktree -- app.js
example.explanation: The first command unstages app.js, the second discards its working-tree edits, and the third replaces its working-tree content with the version from the previous commit.

interview.question: What does git restore change?
interview.answer: git restore updates selected paths in the working tree from a restore source. With --staged it updates the index instead, and --staged --worktree updates both; it does not create a commit or move the branch.
interview.followUp: How would you restore a file from an earlier commit into both locations? Use git restore --source=<commit> --staged --worktree -- <path>.

interview.question: What source does git restore use by default?
interview.answer: For a normal working-tree restore, Git reads the path from the index. For an index restore using --staged, it reads from HEAD unless --source specifies another tree.
interview.followUp: What if the desired contents are from another commit? Add --source=<tree> to select that restore source.

interview.question: How do you unstage a file without discarding its edits?
interview.answer: git restore --staged <path> replaces the index entry with the HEAD version, leaving the working-tree file unchanged. This removes the path from the staged set while preserving the edits in the working tree.
interview.followUp: How can both staged and unstaged contents be replaced? Use --staged --worktree, optionally with --source.

keyPoints: The command restores only the paths you name, copying their content from a selected source into the working tree.
Choose a commit or other tree explicitly with --source when the default index or HEAD is not the desired source.
Combining --staged and --worktree makes the same restore operation affect both the index and working tree.
Restoring can remove a tracked path when that path is absent from the source tree.
gotchas: A tracked path absent from the selected source is deleted when restored.
The default source changes with --staged: HEAD for the index, and the index for the working tree.
Without --staged, the command does not update the index; use the flag to unstage or otherwise replace index content.

Undoing & recovering::git stash.sourceTitle: git-stash - Stash the changes in a dirty working directory away
Undoing & recovering::git stash.summary: Temporarily save the working directory and index as a stash entry, returning them to HEAD so the tree is clean. Inspect, apply, pop, or branch from the saved work later.
Undoing & recovering::git stash.explanation: Git stash records the current state of the working directory and index as a stash entry, then resets them to match HEAD so the working tree is clean. You can inspect entries and restore one later with apply or pop, including onto a different commit.
Undoing & recovering::git stash.syntax:
git stash list [<log-options>]
git stash show [-u | --include-untracked | --only-untracked] [<diff-options>] [<stash>]
git stash drop [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
git stash pop [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
git stash apply [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
git stash branch <branchname> [<stash>]
git stash push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet] [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [-m | --message <message>] [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]] [--] [<pathspec>…]
git stash clear

parameters.name: subcommand/options
parameters.description: Subcommand and options select whether to create, inspect, restore, branch, or remove stash entries; push additionally accepts pathspecs.

Undoing & recovering::git stash.returns: Creates or manipulates stash entries; push saves local modifications and restores the working tree and index to HEAD.

example.title: Save and restore tracked work
example.code:
git init demo && cd demo
git config user.email dev@example.com
git config user.name Dev
printf 'draft\n' > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m 'initial notes'
printf 'more\n' >> notes.txt
git stash push -m 'unfinished notes'
git stash list
git stash pop
example.explanation: Creates a tracked file, modifies it, stores the modification, lists the stash, and restores it.

interview.question: What problem does git stash solve?
interview.answer: git stash saves the current working-directory and index state in a stash entry, then returns both to HEAD. This lets another operation proceed with a clean working tree.
interview.followUp: How can a stash be restored without deleting it? Use git stash apply, optionally selecting an entry and requesting --index.

interview.question: How do apply, pop, list, and show differ?
interview.answer: git stash list displays saved entries, and git stash show inspects an entry. git stash apply restores one while retaining it; git stash pop applies it and then removes it.
interview.followUp: How can a stash be moved to a new branch? Use git stash branch <branchname> [<stash>].

interview.question: Which options control what gets stashed?
interview.answer: The push form accepts options such as --patch, --keep-index, --include-untracked, --all, and --message. These control selection, index handling, untracked files, and the entry description.
interview.followUp: What does --include-untracked change? It includes untracked files in the saved changes, whereas the default operation addresses the tracked working state and index.

keyPoints: Stash captures both unstaged working-tree edits and the index state.
Its main purpose is temporarily removing unfinished work so other Git operations can run cleanly.
Use list to see the available stash entries and their references.
Use show to review an entry and apply to restore it, even when the current commit differs.
The push operation creates a new entry and rolls the saved modifications back to HEAD.
Pop restores a selected entry and can also attempt to restore its staged state with --index.
gotchas: A stash is not opaque: use list to locate entries and show to inspect their changes before restoring them.
Stashing changes the working tree and index back to HEAD; verify that work is safely recorded before continuing.
The bare command is shorthand for push, so use push when you want the operation to be explicit.

Undoing & recovering::git stash pop vs a.summary: `git stash apply` reapplies a stash and keeps its entry; `git stash pop` reapplies it and normally removes the entry. If application conflicts, `pop` leaves the stash available for manual resolution.
Undoing & recovering::git stash pop vs a.explanation: Both commands reapply a selected stash to the current working tree. `apply` leaves the stash entry available, while `pop` attempts the same operation and removes the entry only when application succeeds; conflicts leave it in the stash list for manual resolution and removal.
Undoing & recovering::git stash pop vs a.syntax:
git stash pop [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
git stash apply [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]

parameters.name: --index
parameters.description: Request restoration of the staged state when possible; valid for `pop` and `apply`.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Suppress ordinary command output.

parameters.name: <stash>
parameters.description: The stash entry or stash-like commit to reapply.

Undoing & recovering::git stash pop vs a.returns: Applies the selected stashed state to the current working tree; `pop` also removes the state after successful application, while `apply` retains it. A conflict leaves the state available for manual resolution.

interview.question: What is the practical difference between `git stash pop` and `git stash apply`?
interview.answer: `git stash apply` reapplies the stash but keeps its entry in the stash list. `git stash pop` reapplies it and removes the entry when the application succeeds.
interview.followUp: What happens if `pop` conflicts? The entry remains in the stash list, so resolve the conflict and drop it manually if appropriate.

interview.question: Which arguments can these commands take?
interview.answer: Both accept an optional stash selector, plus `--index` and quiet mode. If no selector is supplied, Git uses the applicable default stash entry.
interview.followUp: Why use `--index`? It asks Git to try to restore the staged state as well as the working-tree changes.

interview.question: How does `pop` behave when applying the stash fails?
interview.answer: A stash application can conflict with the current working tree. With `pop`, a conflict prevents removal, preserving the stash so the changes can be resolved safely.
interview.followUp: How should the preserved entry be handled afterward? Resolve the files manually, then run `git stash drop` when the stash is no longer needed.

keyPoints: The command accepts an optional stash selector, `--index`, and quiet output controls.
`pop` applies one stash to the current working tree and removes that stash after a successful application.
`apply` performs the reapplication without consuming the stash entry.
`apply` can accept a stash-like commit produced by either `stash push` or `stash create`.
The `--index` option is specifically supported for these two stash-reapplication commands.
gotchas: Before using either form, the working directory must match the index.
A conflicting `pop` does not delete the stash; resolve the conflicts and remove the entry manually with `git stash drop`.
After a conflict, resolve files yourself and explicitly run `git stash drop` when the preserved entry is no longer needed.
